entries.title: How Trump Unleashed an Existential Fight Over America's Dinosaurs
entries.summary: In Utah, Trump resurfaced a decades-long dispute over how to protect some of the country’s crown jewels.
entries.content:
Seventy five million years ago, a long-necked creature resembling an oversized ostrich curled into a ball to die.

In June, the dinosaur’s still-curled body took flight over the barren, jagged rocks of southeastern Utah, suspended from the base of a double-rotored military helicopter usually used to airlift tanks.

It was the second helicopter called upon to pull the ornithomimid into the sky. First came a Black Hawk, which struggled to lift the nearly 5,000 pounds of rock and bones. When it failed, state officials sent the far more powerful Chinook, armed with a cadre of soldiers on loan from the National Guard.

Few could see the camouflaged helicopter carrying its bobbing white package for what it was: an animal that once lived among tyrannosaurs and hadrosaurs, set free. Its once marshy wetlands had long since been subsumed by the cliffs that Americans knew until very recently as the Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument.

“Nearly all of the dinosaurs and other fossils preserved in the region have been found nowhere else,” said Joe Sertich, a paleontologist who has studied in Utah for more than a decade.
IMG_3215 copy.jpg (1200x1500, AR: 0.80)Dangling hundreds of feet in the air that summer day was a perfect capsule of that land before time.

Then, just a few weeks after the ornithomimid flew, President Donald Trump declared the dinosaur fossils of Grand Staircase-Escalante “common” and “not unique,” stripping protections from the place where this particular creature had slept for millenia. 


***

Trump shrank the Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument by more than 90% on July 13, removing almost 900,000 acres of geologic layers home to unusually complete dinosaur fossils.

Utah Gov. Spencer Cox and the entirety of the state’s congressional delegation stood behind him in the Oval Office as he signed the proclamation. They applauded, smiled and posed for photographs.

Back home, the scientists and paleontologists who have worked on that land for years sat in disbelief.

“It’s just an absolute distortion of reality to say that the fossils of Grand Staircase are common and can be found anywhere, and therefore don't need any special consideration or protection,” said Alan Titus, who served as Grand Staircase-Escalante’s official monument paleontologist for the Bureau of Land Management until the fall of 2025.

“I so vehemently disagree with that perspective, and I can guarantee the people that wrote it did not talk to a qualified paleontologist about it,” Titus said.

Most of the region’s local leaders disagree with Titus. They love dinosaurs, they say, but the national monument has been a burden. Trump’s order was a long-fought victory, finally giving them more control over the future of both the land — and dinosaurs — they see as theirs.

“The fossils don’t disappear because the boundaries change. That basin is still one of the richest Late Cretaceous ecosystems ever discovered,” said Kaden Figgins, Garfield County’s planning and economic development director.

Figgins believes both that the dinosaurs are an extraordinary resource and that the dramatic cuts to the national monument are a boon for his community.

There are indisputable facts. The fossilized bodies found in Grand Staircase-Escalante are unique. They have inspired massive movie franchises and even amusement parks. The most recent “Jurassic World” featured dinosaurs only known to scientists because of excavations there. Dinosaur species have been found for the first time in this desert.

For the last 15 years, paleontologists and local leaders have been working in tandem to bring that Hollywood attention to their backyard. They want to make Utah a dinosaur capital and build a world-class dinosaur museum — an international destination for scientists and tourists alike.

Trump (8640x5760, AR: 1.50)Monumental Day of Action: Utah based public land rally (4800x3202, AR: 1.50)Then there is the debate. Trump’s proclamation has brought to the surface in Utah a long-simmering and existential disagreement about the future of this land, what it holds and who should control it. The same people who for so long have been united in their belief that the dinosaurs are among the nation’s greatest crown jewels are now fundamentally at odds with each other over what is required to protect them.

In his order, the president did not just dismiss the value of the monument’s scientific resources. He went further, suggesting that the lands could be opened for mining minerals and coal, perhaps helping make the U.S. less dependent on foreign sources of critical minerals.

While the local leaders are excited about what comes with the shrinking of Grand Staircase-Escalante’s boundaries, the researchers are warning that its still-pristine time capsule could be disrupted by industrial development. The dinosaur bones themselves are at greater risk of being stolen and sold on the black market. And without the prestige of a national monument, money for research, a museum or scientific infrastructure will be far harder to secure, they said.

“There needs to be a national dialogue about public lands, and what we want to do with them,” Titus said. “Is this really what we want to do with our public lands? Open them all up to extraction? Or do we want to balance this with conservation, protection, and scientific research?”

Paleontologists believe that this remote corner of southern Utah could be home to the next great undiscovered dinosaur — and the next, and the one after that.

That faith is so strong that one local official is willing to break publicly with his leaders.

State Paleontologist James Kirkland found himself at a loss for words when first asked about Trump’s presidential proclamation. He said that Democrats have sometimes gone too far in their defense of Grand Staircase-Escalante’s massive size. But for the president to attack the monument’s boundaries wholesale? That’s a decision so far beyond his personal red line that he’s willing to risk the consequences of speaking out.

“Yeah we need common sense, but we don’t want to just throw out the baby with the bathwater,” he said. “It’s just sad. We had so much to offer, and this is not going to help anybody.”

"We are talking gigantic dinosaurs,” he went on. “This is the story, the age of dinosaurs in Utah. It could be ground shaking."

***

President Bill Clinton designated Grand Staircase-Escalante as a national monument in 1996. Ever since, researchers in Utah have been discovering new dinosaurs at such a rapid pace they haven’t been able to name them all.

And every year, they dig out at least one especially well-preserved dinosaur. Last year’s dig produced the ornithomimid that scientists airlifted out this summer. The year before it was a tyrannosaur.

“It’s just every year we get something special, like a little baby hadrosaur covered in skin impressions,” said Titus, who retired last year, taking the early resignation offer the Trump administration used to dramatically cut the size of the federal workforce. “It always has a treasure every year. And you don't know what's out there until you go out and look for it.”
IMG_1271 (4032x2688, AR: 1.50)51121918048_68f690813f_o copy.jpg (1620x1080, AR: 1.50)Unlike many of the better-known dinosaur hotspots in China, and even in North America, Grand Staircase-Escalante is still in the early stages of investigation, paleontologists said.

Even researchers from China — often credited with the most interesting dinosaurs yet known to man — have come to see the fossils of Grand Staircase-Escalante.

“The Chinese admit we have the best Mesozoic age of dinosaurs record anywhere in the world,” Kirkland said.

Discoveries have come thick and fast in recent years only because researchers finally had access to modern tools and transportation. The region, known as the Kaiparowits Plateau, is so remote that it was the last part of the contiguous United States reached by cartographers.

The Chinook that carried the ornithomimid in June was merely the most recent helicopter deputized for dinosaur transport. The fossils are so massive that in previous years, paleontologists have paid federal wildland firefighting teams to swing by with their helicopters at the end of a deployment to pick up bones.

“We’ll fly a camp deep into the backcountry and camp out there for two or three weeks,” Sertich said.

Because the digs are especially expensive, funding them has become increasingly difficult as research dollars grow scarce. Paleontologists have relied heavily on the Grand Staircase-Escalante name to help get the limited dollars flowing over the last two decades, they said. Without that monument status to attract attention, they predicted that resources that were already hard to tap will likely grow dry.

“The new executive order cuts us off at the knees in that effort” to make Utah a new epicenter for dinosaur study and tourism, Titus said. The Interior Department has not hired anyone to replace him as the monument paleontologist at the Bureau of Land Management.

A BLM spokesperson told The Washington Sun that paleontological resources and protection "is not limited to areas with monument designation.”

“BLM Utah will move forward with advertising the position as opportunity and funds become available,” the spokesperson said.

The region’s local leaders share Titus’ passion for the dinosaurs. Several told The Sun that no other place on Earth can compete with what’s been found in their backyards.

One official went so far as to say that the county’s great exports are twofold: “our children and our dinosaurs.”

But they don’t have Titus’ fear for the future. In fact, these local leaders said that they don’t believe there’s any risk at all in cutting the monument.

***

The contours of today’s fight trace back to at least 1976, when a group of power companies abandoned plans to build what at the time would have been the largest coal power plant in the country on the edge of the Kaiparowits Plateau. The plant would have been powered by coal blasted out of the same rocks that hold the fossils.

Back then, no one understood that there was an expansive dinosaur boneyard in those rocks. The plan fell apart because mining in the region was plagued with problems.

Mining the region was just as fraught in the 1990s, when another plan coalesced to build a coal mine in the middle of the plateau. But that time, the project died because Clinton established the national monument, effectively making it impossible to move forward. In the process, Utah Republicans grew increasingly angry with the federal government’s power over public lands; on the day of the monument designation ceremony, both Clinton and then-Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt were hung in effigy from lampposts in Escalante.
PRESIDENT CLINTON (1790x1430, AR: 1.25)Exactly 30 years after they sent black balloons into the sky and told The New York Times that “We’ve had it up to here with the federal government,” Utah’s local Republicans have freed the land from the monument.

But now they face a new challenge. The intervening three decades’ worth of research have irrevocably altered understanding of what’s inside those rocks in Grand Staircase-Escalante. Even if mining the plateau today is economically justifiable and technically feasible — questions as yet unanswered — any new mining effort would have to confront what could be lying on top of a possible uranium deposit.

Federal laws like the National Paleontological Resource Preservation Act, which prohibits anyone from taking fossils with vertebrae from federal lands, will remain in effect. The Bureau of Land Management's “legal responsibilities for paleontological resources did not change with the monument’s boundaries,” the BLM spokesperson said. “Vertebrate fossils are protected across all BLM‑administered lands, regardless of monument designation,”

But those laws are rarely enforced, Titus and Sertich said.

It is the land’s monument status, and the special protections that come with it — like the complete prohibition on taking anything out of the monument — that do far more to guarantee the safety of the dinosaurs in the long term, Sertich insisted.

Utah’s local leaders who advocated shrinking the monument say the dinosaurs aren’t at all at risk; if anything, they say, Trump’s order will boost their push for a regional museum.

“We hope it does bring attention to what’s there,” said Dave Dodds, the Garfield County public works director, arguing that shrinking the monument would lead to greater focus on what remains. “We hope that this can focus in on the dinosaurs down there.”

Garfield County Commissioner Jerry Taylor has been trying to get the museum off the ground for a long time; he had a feasibility study commissioned, he consulted experts who helped design North America’s most famous dinosaur museums, and he even recently persuaded the Utah State Legislature to provide a small amount of seed funding.

The presence of the monument has not helped advance those efforts, Dodds and Figgins said.

“We’ve never received federal funding for this, and we’ve been begging for 20 years,” Figgins said. “The museum does not exist because it was the Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument. The museum exists because it’s one of the most significant dinosaur discovery regions in North America.”

The Bureau of Land Management said the government’s existing partnerships with universities and museums, and its work to “expand statewide capacity for preparation, curation, and research,” would be “unaffected by monument boundary changes.”

The government currently has partnerships with Utah State University Eastern’s Prehistoric Museum and the Natural History Museum of Utah.

***

The most legendary dinosaur quarry in Grand Staircase-Escalante is called “Rainbows and Unicorns.”

It’s there that in 2014 Titus discovered a family of tyrannosaurs that drowned in a flood together, all of them unusually intact. Paleontologists are still studying these massive creatures, hoping to answer the many questions that arose from their discovery more than a decade ago: Were tyrannosaurs actually social creatures, traveling in groups with their relatives? Are these fossils an entirely new species of tyrannosaur?

Rainbows and Unicorns is the single fossil-rich area that Trump protected when he shrank the monument in July, calling it “a globally important paleontological resource.”
IMG_1167.JPG (4032x2863, AR: 1.41)IMG_0388.JPG (4032x3024, AR: 1.33)There was a deep irony in that for Sertich: The president kept protections for the one place where the most impressive fossils had already been found and largely removed from the site.

“Of course there are still bones in the ground, but you know the important stuff has already been excavated and removed, so now they're preserving largely a hole in the ground,” he said.

There are hundreds of thousands of acres across the Kaiparowits Plateau with the potential for equally impressive finds, paleontologists said — and now they are no longer protected by monument status.

The researchers who have devoted their lives to this work have a nagging fear that if they don’t find and study these bones themselves, the fossils could end up one day on display in a private compound instead of a museum in Utah.

“We’ve cracked the door on the safe over the last 30 years, and now people want fossils for themselves. There’s a whole underground market for illegal fossils, and I see these things pop up on Instagram and eBay all the time. That’s going to become rampant,” Sertich said.

Enthusiasm for dinosaurs is exploding globally, with or without Utah riding along. A tyrannosaurus known as Gus sold for $50 million in an official auction in July, and the black market is growing quickly in response to the demand.

The Bureau of Land Management’s “law enforcement responsibilities remain in place,” the agency’s spokesperson said.

Titus has in the past been involved in efforts to prosecute the thieves. But in certain parts of the Western United States, black market collectors have grown systematic and organized in their dinosaur looting, Titus said.

That level of sophistication has not yet reached Grand Staircase-Escalante. Still, he wonders if that’s only a matter of time in a world increasingly obsessed with the best possible fossils.

“The bad guys know that now they can go out there and just pretend they are looking for clamshells,” he said.

entries.title: What to Do in the D.C. Area This Weekend (Sept. 10)
entries.summary: Go see a John Philip Sousa ballet or take your dog to visit the composer’s grave.
entries.content:
Thursday 


Philadelphia Ballet at Wolf Trap 

Filene Center, 1551 Trap Road, Vienna, 8 p.m., $42 to $133

The Philadelphia Ballet brings a full-firepower performance of four ballets set to American music: Jerome Robbins’ “Fancy Free,” Eliot Feld’s “Variations on America,” George Balanchine’s “Who Cares?” and John Philip Sousa’s “Stars and Stripes Forever.” Con: There’s no live orchestra playing Sousa. Pros: Jane Raleigh, the beloved former dance director of the Kennedy Center, will lead a panel discussion before the show, and one kid can come free with the purchase of each adult ticket.

Brazil Independence Day celebration at El Mercat Bar de Tapas

1301 S. Joyce St., Arlington, 7 p.m., $10 cover charge 

Fiesta D.C., the same group organizing a Latino festival and parade for Sept. 26 and 27, starts the Latin American Heritage Month party early with a celebration of Brazil’s Independence Day. Join the Vavá United School of Samba for an evening of tapas, music and samba lessons in Pentagon City.

More to explore: “Love Letters of World War II,” a free music and dance performance at the Library of Congress

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Friday 


“The Score” at Shakespeare Theatre

610 F St. NW, 7:30 p.m., $43 to 152. Runs through Oct. 25.

Every “Succession” fan’s favorite patriarch is coming to town to play Baroque composer Johann Sebastian Bach. Instead of his small-screen offspring, however, Scottish actor Brian Cox faces off against Prussian monarch Frederick the Great. Cox’s wife, Nicole Ansari, stars opposite him as Anna Magdalena Bach, mother to 13 of the composer’s 20 children. A Guardian critic deemed the script uneven when the drama debuted in England three years ago, but had high praise for Cox, “who plays the genius musician with such magnetism that he almost singlehandedly saves this play.”

The Folger Consort performs “Monteverdi’s Legacy”

Folger Shakespeare Library, 201 East Capital St. SE, 8 p.m., $20 to $50. Additional performances Saturday and Sunday. 

Meanwhile, at the other Shakespeare-centric theater in town, the Folger Consort opens its 50th season with a program billed as “the musical equivalent of a gondola tour through 17th-century Venice.” Consort co-founder Robert Eisenstein will play music of Monteverdi and his successors on the viola da gamba, joined by two sopranos and four other musicians.

More to explore: Opening night of the NoMa in Color Mural Festival

Saturday 


Gin Dance Company’s Farewell Performance

Capital One Hall, 7750 Capital One Tower Road, Tysons, 7:30 p.m., $61.75

Choreographer Shu-Chen Cuff’s personal story is the stuff of American dreams: After immigrating to the U.S. from Taiwan, she graduated from the prestigious New World School of the Arts. She landed a job with Nevada Ballet Theatre, but found dancing didn’t pay the bills. She sold watches on the side, met and married a customer, and followed her new husband to Fairfax. For 15 years, Gin Dance has been an artistic home for many young professionals with high levels of training but day jobs in other fields. Now she’s retiring from running the company. Four works and 14 dancers are on the final program.

“Come From Away” at Ford’s Theatre

511 10th St., 7:30 p.m., $20 to $110. Runs through Oct. 18.

The concept sounded improbable and perhaps even crass: a docu-dramedy musical about Sept. 11? Yet “Come From Away” has become one of the most popular musicals of the 21st century. Ford’s Theatre marks the 25th anniversary of 9/11 with a reprise of the musical, which stopped in D.C. ahead of its long Broadway run. Opening-night guests in 2016 included Elaine Chao, Sen. Rand Paul and the mayor of Gander, Newfoundland, a character in the show. After the Twin Towers fell, the town welcomed the passengers of 38 stranded planes. Now the musical about Canadian generosity takes the stage against the backdrop of President Donald Trump’s tariff war.

More to explore: The 34th annual Rosslyn Jazz Fest

Sunday 


Adams Morgan Day

18th Street and Columbia Road, noon to 6 p.m., free

The neighborhood that remains home to some of the District’s quirkiest indoor establishments — animal crackers at Tryst or redhead night at Madam’s Organ, anyone? — pours out onto the streets Sunday. This volunteer-run festival has a catch-as-catch-can vibe, but everyone should stumble into something fun. Scheduled events include “Volo Kids” activity zone from noon to 2 p.m. and a 1 p.m. mural unveiling at 1640 Columbia Road. Entertainment ranges from Civil War reenactors to FrankoJazz karaoke to Cuban dance troupe D.C. Casineros.

“Congressional Unleashed” Pet Tour at Historic Congressional Cemetery

1801 E St. SE, 1 p.m., $10 

This guided tour for history buffs focuses on famous animal lovers interred in the 200-year-old cemetery. Among those to whom you and your pet may pay respects: “Stars and Stripes Forever” composer John Philip Sousa, journalist Cokie Roberts and Minnesota explorer Joseph Nicollet. Note that Americans with complex legacies, such as Lincoln conspirator David Herold and FBI Director J. Edgar Hoover, are also buried in Congressional Cemetery; peeing on gravestones may result in you (and your pet) being banned from the premises.

More to explore: 41st annual Mediterranean Festival at Saints Peter and Paul Antiochian Orthodox Christian Church in Potomac

entries.title: Are Maryland Drivers as Bad as Everyone in D.C. Thinks?
entries.summary: We looked at a decade of crash data to figure out which drivers truly rank as the District’s most dangerous.
entries.content:
Jeff Dooley, a Virginia native and current D.C. resident who runs The Washington Sun’s local and sports coverage, asked if we could confirm the D.C. region’s most enduring stereotype: Are Maryland drivers really the worst?

At first glance, the data seemed to confirm our suspicions.

A quick analysis of crash and license-plate data from D.C.’s Metropolitan Police Department reveals something genuinely impressive: From 2019 to 2021, Maryland drivers were at fault in more two-car crashes in D.C. than drivers from anywhere else, including D.C. Those are the most recent years for which we have good numbers. The picture gets fuzzy in 2021 as the D.C. government appears to have tapped the brakes on releasing detailed license-plate data.

But is that an unfair assessment? Could it be that there are just more Maryland drivers on District roads?

Of course there are. Of D.C. workers who commute by car, almost half (48%) drove in from Maryland between 2022 and 2024. Another 30% drove from Virginia, and only 21% were D.C. residents, according to our analysis of the Census Bureau’s American Community Survey.

DCdrivers online notus-03.png (3034x945, AR: 3.21)
How do we account for that? We tried some surprisingly simple math. We compared the share of accidents involving a driver with Maryland plates who’s at fault — meaning they were ticketed for an offense that could have caused an accident, such as running a red light, making an illegal U-turn or going the wrong way on a one-way street — to the share of Maryland drivers who were the unoffending party in a two-car accident.

When we did that, Maryland drivers didn't look so bad. They’re only slightly more likely to be at fault in an accident as they are to be innocent victims, according to our analysis of about a decade of MPD data ending in 2021.

That still makes them worse than D.C. drivers, who are over 15% less likely to be at fault than to be the victim. But they both do far better than drivers from Virginia, who are over 20% more likely to be at fault. Drivers from outside the region fare even worse, but they’re rarer on the District’s roads and thus don’t feature as prominently in local stereotypes.

DCdrivers online notus_Graphic.png (3034x2195, AR: 1.38)But before declaring D.C. drivers excellent, Maryland drivers exonerated and Virginia drivers the actual villains, we checked in with our colleagues. Right away, legendary District-knower Martin Austermuhle kindly reminded us that D.C. and Maryland drivers have been known to cross the river for cheaper Virginia plates, since the state has low fees and no residency requirement.

The dodge became less lucrative once Virginia began requiring insurance in 2024, but it appears to remain popular among folks looking to save a few bucks and maybe avoid Maryland inspections or fines. But Maryland is cracking down — beginning in October, a new law will fine residents with out-of-state plates.

D.C. has its own rules limiting outside plates, but D.C. licensed drivers remain far more likely to have out-of-state plates than drivers in any state in the country, according to our quick analysis of a decade of data from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s Fatality Analysis Reporting System.

Of all D.C. licensed drivers involved in fatal accidents, almost half (46%) were on out-of-state plates, compared with just 12% for the highest states. Drivers in deadly crashes probably differ meaningfully from the population at large, but it’s safe to assume D.C. remains unique by any measure.

https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/pgG99/1/Unfortunately, we can’t directly correct for out-of-state drivers. The MPD data released by the District Department of Transportation only tells us the state of the license plate, not the state the at-fault driver is licensed in. They did, however, release both license-state and plate-state data for more than 27,000 drivers involved in crashes that resulted in moving violations between 2016 and 2020.

And that data has one clear message: Don’t trust Virginia plates! More than a third (35%) of drivers cited by police with Virginia plates actually had licenses from other states. That’s about double the comparable number for Maryland drivers (17%).

So, what would D.C. data look like if we only measured “real” Virginia drivers? We can’t know. MPD doesn’t release enough driver’s license data. But we can guess based on better data from the District’s northern and eastern suburbs, courtesy of the Maryland State Police. It comes from different years — 2024 to 2026 — so it’s not a perfect comparison, but it’s the best we have.

In Montgomery and Prince George’s counties, drivers with Virginia plates look like absolute menaces, about 25% and 35% more likely to be at fault, respectively. But if you only look at drivers with Virginia licenses, the discrepancy effectively vanishes — they’re only slightly more likely to be the at-fault driver.

Why might D.C.-region drivers with Virginia plates be so much more reckless on the road? We’re guessing it’s partly explained by the clearest trend in the data. Young drivers — those under age 25 — are much, much more likely to be at fault in an accident in D.C., as will already be obvious to anyone who’s tried to insure a college student and/or knew us in our 20s.
DCdrivers online notus-02.png (3034x1254, AR: 2.42)
In related news, those potemkin Virginians tend to be younger than drivers whose plates match their state. This makes sense, as cars with Virginia plates have long been cheaper to register and insure, and thus popular with the region’s impecunious youth. It also may explain their apparent recklessness.

In other words, the more we dug into the data, the more our gut impression shifted. We can’t say anything cohesive when faced with such balkanized numbers, but our feeling is that you might drive a bit more safely on your home roads, and maybe a bit more risk when you’re far from home, but those rules apply to everybody. Regardless of the state, drivers are roughly the same.

So it’s reasonable to drive defensively when you spot Virginia or out-of-state plates in D.C., but you can’t really blame actual Virginians. If you’re stereotyping anyone, it should probably be younger drivers, regardless of what state their plates come from.

entries.title: Sam Altman Privately Rejected Giving OpenAI Shares to the Government
entries.summary: The remarks follow months of reports connecting Altman to the idea of giving the government equity in his company.
entries.content:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman privately told a group of conservatives this summer that he did not support having the government take shares in the company, distancing himself from a proposal that he and his firm were widely understood to have supported.

For months, OpenAI has been connected to the idea that it is interested in voluntarily ceding shares to the government. Altman has spoken to senior Trump administration officials about the idea, as The Washington Sun first reported in June. The Financial Times reported that OpenAI had proposed giving the government a 5 percent stake in the company, citing Altman’s private comments. The New York Times wrote that Altman had directly pitched President Donald Trump on creating a “government investment fund” seeded with shares in OpenAI. And The Associated Press reported that Altman told Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) that he wants the public to have equity in artificial intelligence companies.

At the off-record meeting with conservative economists on July 29, Altman said that he supports some version of redistributing company shares to the American public, according to three people present and notes taken by one participant reviewed by The Washington Sun. But he also was adamant that he would oppose the government taking equity in his firm and would resist any efforts for federal control over the company, those in the room said.

Altman’s comments, previously unreported, provide new insight about the intentions of the leader of one of the most powerful technology companies in the world, as companies like his own and Anthropic navigate public backlash against the rise of AI.

To those present, Altman appeared confused why anyone could think he wanted the government to take shares in the company.

"To most people in Washington, 'public shares in OpenAI' obviously means government control," said one of the economists who attended the meeting. “But he did not seem to understand that and seemed confused that anyone would think that’s what it meant. He said, 'That's not what we're talking about.' … I had the sense that he did not see as big of a difference between individual Americans owning shares and the government owning shares as there is in reality.”

The economists spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe the off-record discussion.

In a statement to The Sun, the company said it supported creating a “government-administered public wealth fund,” which it distinguished from one in which the government took a “controlling or ownership stake in AI companies, which we would not support.”

"We think AI should create economic opportunity for everyone,” the statement said. “In April, we published an industrial policy blueprint with several ideas, including a public wealth fund that would let people share directly in the economic gains from AI. We’ve also talked with policymakers in both parties about related ideas, including whether AI companies could contribute equity to help seed a fund, but we are not close to anything specific.”

Several experts expressed confusion about Altman’s position. Theoretically, it would be possible for OpenAI to at some point donate “nonvoting” shares to a private entity overseen in part by government officials, which would limit federal control over the firm. But this would still amount to ceding stakes to the government.

"Everything we've seen from Sam Altman and OpenAI over the years implied a pretty conventional government ownership stake in the companies, including voting rights, dividend rights, other kinds of shareholder rights," said Matt Bruenig, founder of the People's Policy Project, a left-leaning think tank. "The distinction they are drawing is hard to understand: How does a government-administered public wealth fund that owns equity not have an ownership stake in companies? These sentences are contradictory."

The position also diverges from that understood by others in Washington who have met with Altman. In a meeting in Sanders’ office in late June, Altman said he had seen the senator’s bill requiring AI giants to turn over 50 percent of their shares to the government and agreed that the government should have some stake in the AI companies, though not 50 percent, according to another person familiar with the matter, who also spoke on the condition of anonymity to recount that private discussion.

By contrast, the economists who attended the July 29 meeting came away from the discussion with Altman believing that OpenAI agreed with their fierce opposition to expanding the government’s control over the private sector.

Some experts have long been skeptical that OpenAI really would be voluntarily willing to turn over what would amount to billions of dollars to the government. Jeremy Bearer-Friend, an AI expert and law professor at George Washington University who helped design the Sanders plan, said there is nothing in corporate law currently stopping Altman from ceding shares to the government.

Shareholders could sue the company if it made that decision, but it would have the freedom to try.

“They already could have done it,” Bearer-Friend said.

The same day Altman met with conservative economic policy experts, the OpenAI executive also briefed a group of economists influential with Democratic policymakers. Several attendees of that second meeting did not recall the equity stakes question being discussed.

Both meetings started with presentations from Altman about the mathematical breakthroughs made by the OpenAI models. To the conservative economists, Altman stressed that OpenAI had the least politically biased model of any of the major AI companies, two of the people at that meeting said. The liberal economists did not remember Altman discussing the political orientation of the OpenAI model.

entries.title: Republicans Gather for Two-Day 'Trump-a-Palooza' Midterm Convention
entries.summary: Many party members, including those facing tight races, are skipping the entire affair.
entries.content:
By Jill Colvin

NEW YORK (AP) — Republicans are gathering in Dallas on Wednesday for a highly unusual midterm convention, a “Trump-a-Palooza” that will put President Donald Trump at the center of this fall’s midterm elections — whether the candidates running like it or not.

Many party members, including those facing tight races, are skipping the two-day affair, citing conflicting obligations or balking at demands that they pony up for access. Others are hoping an appearance alongside Trump will put them in the national spotlight as they work to turn out his voters without him on the ballot.

The convention, which is part rally and part fundraiser, comes as Republicans try to boost enthusiasm heading into the midterms’ final stretch despite Trump’s low approval ratings. Organizers have cast it as “a primetime showcase for President Trump’s success, candidates, and causes that have propelled the 2026 midterms to unprecedented focus.” Much of the programming will focus on Democrats, trying to cast them as extremists by highlighting the party’s insurgent left wing.

The lineup features Trump and more Trump

Normal political conventions are held every four years and serve a purpose beyond pomp and circumstance, with parties formally nominating their presidential picks. In 2024, Trump used the opportunity to announce JD Vance as his running mate.

The schedule this week released by organizers makes clear that the convention will be the Trump Show, through and through.

“It’s gonna be a Trump-a-Palooza,” RNC Chairman Joe Gruters told Spectrum News.

The president will be speaking both nights, delivering a keynote address on Wednesday night and speaking again Thursday after Vance to close out the event. He had originally been scheduled for only one speaking slot.

Also addressing the convention will be members of the Republican congressional leadership and Cabinet members including Attorney General Todd Blanche and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. The president’s oldest son, Donald Trump Jr., is on the roster, too.

Candidates who will speak include Michigan Senate nominee Mike Rogers, who is running a high-profile race against Abdul El-Sayed, and North Carolina Senate nominee Michael Whatley, who is up against former Gov. Roy Cooper.

Organizers have outlined 12 hours of programming over the two nights that will include more than 100 speakers and segments focused on subjects like tax cuts, fraud allegations, border security and a proposed ban on members of Congress trading stocks.

Missing from the public lineup: any mention of the unpopular war with Iran.

Republican House Speaker Mike Johnson said some members of his caucus plan to skip Dallas, preferring to stay home and campaign for reelection, but many of them will make an appearance.

“We’ll parade our stars across the stage,” he said.

Many will be skipping the event

An Associated Press survey of more than four dozen Republican candidates found a majority either planned not to attend, said their plans were to be determined, or ignored requests for comment.

“I had stuff already planned in my congressional district or I would be there,” Kentucky Rep. James Comer told NewsNation. “Got a lot going on back in Kentucky, so my time is needed there.”

“Well, unfortunately, I have a family obligation, so I won’t be able to be there,” Georgia Rep. Buddy Carter said on Fox Business.

Some members balked at high attendance fees. Republican House members were being asked to pay $25,000 for convention tickets and lodging, according to a person familiar with the situation and granted anonymity to speak frankly about the private arrangement.

An additional 2,000 tickets were distributed by the House GOP’s campaign arm, largely to donors and others to attend the convention. Other tickets were allocated to state parties to distribute as they saw fit.

“Per the RNC, this is a ticketed fundraiser and rally, not a traditional national convention,” the Denton County Republican Party in Texas wrote in a Facebook post, which advertised packages from $5,000 to $20,000.

The Republican Party of Virginia was offering a relative discount of $1,000 to $1,500, not including accommodations, according to an email obtained by the AP.

Despite the many no-shows, more than 100 Republican House members and candidates are expected to be in Dallas, including almost all of the MAGA Majority class of candidates in the most targeted congressional districts, according to a person familiar with the event who requested anonymity before it begins.

“It’s like any political convention, it’s no different than the traditional RNC,” said Matt Beynon, a spokesperson for Pennsylvania Rep. Scott Perry, who won his district by barely 1 percentage point in 2024 with Trump on the ballot. “Obviously, you’re out of the district, but it’s a really good opportunity to get in front of people” and “talk to the press.”

It remains unclear what kind of air time the convention will receive. The two nights of programming will coincide with the launch of football season. The NFL season is set to kick off Wednesday with a game between the Seattle Seahawks and the New England Patriots. And on Thursday, the San Francisco 49ers and Los Angeles Rams will be playing an international game in Australia.

Democrats say Republicans are out of touch

Democrats, meanwhile, are planning their own counterprogramming.

“The fact that these Republicans are planning a celebration in the middle of an economic crisis — where everyday Americans are drowning because of this high cost of living — is extraordinary,” Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, the House Democratic leader, said at the U.S. Capitol.

Democrats have held such midterm conventions in the past but are not doing so this year. Rep. Suzan DelBene of Washington, chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, said she wasn’t worried that her party was missing an opportunity to make its case on a national stage like Republicans.

“They are not focused on the issues that people are struggling with right now, that they’ve created," DelBene said. “Cost, housing, food, healthcare, childcare, energy costs, gas prices all going up. That’s what we’re talking about on the ground all across the country.”

Americans “are going to continue to see how much they don’t care,” she added. "And we’re gonna be on the ground all across the country with great candidates talking directly to the American people.”

Associated Press writers Steven Sloan, Marc Levy, Lisa Mascaro and Sarah Rankin contributed to this report.

entries.title: Trump Gave Hefty Holiday Bonuses to Natalie Harp and Other Aides
entries.summary: The bonuses were $45,000 each and marked as a “cash gift” for the holidays.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump gave hefty holiday bonuses to several White House aides, including his executive assistant Natalie Harp, financial disclosures released by the Trump administration on Tuesday show.

The bonuses totaled $45,000 each and were given to Harp and two other young staffers — communications adviser Margo Martin and Deputy Director of Oval Office Operations Chamberlain Harris.

The financial disclosure forms also show that Harp, Martin and Harris each receive a $150,000 salary. The bonuses were marked as a “Cash Gift for the Holidays” on the disclosure forms.

Director of Oval Office operations Walt Nauta also received a $20,000 bonus, according to the disclosure forms. He makes $175,000 a year.

The White House said in a statement that Trump has a longstanding practice of giving Christmas gifts to people in his orbit, both while working in government and during his time in the private sector.

“The gifts at issue here have nothing to do with any of these individuals’ official government duties, and therefore are entirely permissible under relevant legal and ethical standards,” a White House official said.

Harp has come under increased scrutiny over the last few months for her position at the White House. She is known as Trump’s “human printer” and carries around a portable device to provide Trump with hard copies of flattering news articles and social media posts.

The 35-year-old was one of few staffers that accompanied Trump on a catering truck as he secretly swapped planes to fly from Turkey to the United States in July, The Washington Post reported.

There is no apparent precedent for U.S. presidents giving staff employed by the White House large cash payments.

entries.title: Argument Over Grooming Standards Led to D.C. National Guard Gun Incident: Docs
entries.summary: The 21-year-old service member hails from Georgia and is stationed in D.C. as part of the president’s efforts to crack down on crime in the district.
entries.content:
A National Guard member from Georgia is facing felony charges after being accused of brandishing his gun at another service member during an argument over Army grooming standards, according to witness reports and an arrest affidavit.

More than 3,000 troops are currently stationed in D.C. to combat what President Donald Trump has called “the destructive forces of criminal activity” in Washington. The troops have been in the District since August 2025, and Trump recently extended their deployment until 2029.

On Aug. 25, a group of Guard members were “sitting in their black van in front of Popeyes” on H Street while they took a break from patrol, court documents said. Zion Mitchell, 21, was seated in the rear row of the vehicle when he got into an argument with a soldier seated in the right front passenger seat, according to the filings.

Mitchell allegedly pulled out his service weapon, held it over another guard’s shoulder and aimed it at the accuser, an affidavit from the Superior Court of the District of Columbia said.

Mitchell was charged with assault with a dangerous weapon and possession of a firearm during a crime of violence on Sept. 1.

Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Several witness accounts of the incident said that Mitchell and the accuser “were engaged in an argument over their hairstyles and whether they were following Army regulations” — standards that underwent significant changes last month.

Mitchell described the argument as “playful” in his interview with police, but the accuser said she told Mitchell to “shut the fuck up” during the altercation.

The soldier then claimed she heard a “holster click,” and said that witnesses later informed her that Mitchell had drawn his weapon. She believed that the firearm in question was loaded, “since all the National Guard's firearms are generally loaded,” and a witness later confirmed that it had a live round in the chamber.

When asked why he brandished his weapon, Mitchell told a witness, “It doesn't matter, it was on safe," according to the arrest record.

With National Guard members deployed to Washington from 18 states, Puerto Rico and D.C., some D.C. residents have gotten used to the presence of armed troops in their neighborhood — while others are still calling for them to be sent home. The National Guard members in D.C. are disproportionately in their late teens and early 20s, and roughly 60% come from Republican-led Southern states.
entries.author: Jenna Monnin

entries.title: Metro Is Rolling Out New Train Station Signs
entries.summary: The change will make it easier to update signs in the future, Metro said. But many riders expressed displeasure on social media.
entries.content:
Metro is updating signage at each rail station in an attempt to make it easier for customers to navigate D.C.

Riders at L’Enfant Plaza may have noticed fresh signs on the lower train platforms, the first in what is planned to be a systemwide rollout of new directional signage across D.C. Metrorail. The changes are meant to make traveling “clearer and more consistent,” according to Metro’s website.

Exits will no longer be labeled by the street intersections they lead to, but rather a letter — A, B, C, etc. — that corresponds to attractions near each exit, such as the Wharf and the International Spy Museum at L’Enfant. Graphics showing the remaining stops on each line will be taken off the wall of each terminal, relegating full route information to signs on the platform.
HTML EmbedThe change will make it easier and cheaper to update signs in the future, according to Metro’s website.

But riders pushed back on social media, saying the new signs are less intuitive and make information harder to find.

“It may seem unfamiliar at first glance, but multiple rounds of feedback were considered to finalize this effort. The results are exciting — a clearer set of signs to address navigation decisions at key decision points,” Metro said in a social media post.

Metro did not immediately respond to questions about the new rollout.

Some signs at L’Enfant have already been switched, with the station expected to have completely new placards by the end of October. Within the next six months, five more stations will be updated. Metro’s website said every station will be updated within five years.

Beyond new signage inside the station, the pylons marking Metro train station entrances will ditch the iconic striped top design, opting instead for colored circles denoting rail lines down the side.

entries.title: Aide Who Blew the Whistle on Paxton Backs Talarico in Splashy Ad Campaign
entries.summary: The Texas law enforcement official reported Paxton to the FBI in 2020 for misusing the attorney general’s office.
entries.content:
A former top aide to Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton who reported his former boss to the FBI is throwing his support behind state Rep. James Talarico’s Senate campaign.

“Ken Paxton ended my five decade career because I blew the whistle on his corruption,” David Maxwell said in the minute-long campaign ad released Tuesday.

David Maxwell served in Texas law enforcement for nearly 50 years, and he spent close to a decade working as the director of law enforcement for the attorney general’s office.

The former Texas Ranger isn’t the first person with previously close ties to Paxton who has decided to endorse Talarico. In June, Talarico’s campaign reported that Paxton’s impeachment trial attorney, Dan Cogdell, decided to back the Democratic nominee for Senate.

Maxwell’s lengthy law enforcement career helps him know “a bad guy when he sees one,” the campaign ad says.

In 2020, after working with Paxton for over half a decade, Maxwell and a group of other top staffers reported him to the FBI for allegedly misusing the attorney general’s office and doing personal favors for Nate Paul — a real estate developer and political donor to Paxton.

Paxton’s ties to Paul led the Texas state House to launch formal proceedings against Paxton, who faced more than a dozen articles of impeachment, including making false statements and misuse of public resources. In 2023, the House voted to impeach Paxton, but he was later acquitted by the state Senate and allowed to return to his post as attorney general.

Paxton fired Maxwell and some of the other aides months after their report. In April 2025, a Texas judge ordered Paxton to pay Maxwell and four of the whistleblowers $6.6 million after they filed a lawsuit against the attorney general.

The negative campaign ads have ramped up in recent weeks in what’s now rated a “toss up” election that both parties see as a must-win Senate seat.

Talarico’s campaign has capitalized on Maxwell’s story and other legal trouble Paxton has faced to paint him as an untrustworthy candidate.

Last month, the Democrat’s campaign released an ad slamming Paxton for taking a $1,000 Montblanc pen from a security screening area at a Texas courthouse in 2012. Although Paxton eventually returned the pen, its owner, attorney Joe Joplin, endorsed Talarico in the ad.

Paxton has also run his share of attack ads against Talarico, often claiming his opponent holds a “radical agenda.” The Republican nominee released an AI-generated ad on Tuesday of Talarico repeating some of his past controversial comments on Christianity and religion out of context.

entries.title: Abdul El-Sayed Says It’s Time to ‘Pause’ AI Development
entries.summary: The Michigan Democrat calls for a pause and admits his initial approach didn’t account for the speed of the new technology.
entries.content:
Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is calling for a pause on AI development after warnings from Anthropic researchers that it could destroy humans this decade, calling it a “break glass moment.”

“I think now we're in a situation where time is of the essence,” El-Sayed said Wednesday in an exclusive interview with The Washington Sun. “The speed at which this is all progressing is really quite alarming, considering the fact that they've taken on capacities we did not know were previously possible.”

The debate over the rapid development of data centers required for AI development is a major flash point in the midterm elections, but Congress hasn’t done much to address concerns.

El-Sayed, who’s running against Michigan Republican Mike Rogers in November, released an AI plan earlier this summer calling for public ownership of artificial intelligence and strict safety rules. He told The Sun that it’s now time to go further.

“I think it's important for us to really hit pause, hit pause in a serious way, and fully understand what it is that is being built when it has so much potential spillover into irreversible damage for humanity,” he added.

Fears about the rapid pace of AI development have escalated sharply following recent incidents involving rogue AI agents. On Tuesday, several Anthropic researchers went public with serious concerns about the industry.

"The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” AI researcher Jacob Coxon wrote in a social media post announcing his resignation from the company. “This is not a marketing stunt. If anything, many executives and senior researchers will couch their phrasing in the press to sound sensible - but I hear the same people express fear privately. No other human activity poses this level of danger."

Anthropic alignment-science lead Evan Hubinger responded by agreeing with Coxon, putting the odds of humanity’s extinction at greater than 10%.

“I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to,” Hubinger said.

These are only the latest warnings about AI. Earlier this week, OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki warned that AI capabilities are advancing faster than researchers’ ability to reliably monitor and control them. In July, nearly 1,400 AI company employees signed an open letter urging the U.S. government to regulate the technology.

Policymakers have been slow to respond.

President Donald Trump last month declared the U.S. should “let Data Reign,” criticizing towns and states that reject AI data centers. In Congress, Republicans have broadly cheered AI development, while Democrats have mostly focused on oversight and safeguards. Progressive Sen. Bernie Sanders, an independent from Vermont, went furthest by calling for a moratorium on new data center construction and a pause on advanced AI development.

Still, there are signs of bipartisan appetite for stronger AI regulation.

Rep. Anna Paulina Luna, a Republican from Florida, called on Congress to convene “a special session on AI and what the future of the U.S. looks like.”

“There are very real impacts to society as we know it. Partisan politics aside, there are massive implications of a race towards super intelligence. This is not a doomer post, as some of the advancements will greatly impact access to healthcare, targeted treatments, increase in safer food production etc… but not enough of Congress is focusing on this,” Luna wrote Wednesday in a social media post.

El-Sayed, a progressive Democrat who’s been backed by Sanders, also said it’s time to take more drastic steps to ensure AI doesn’t lead to economic and societal catastrophe.

“AI is truly a life altering technology. The question for us is: In what way does it alter our lives?” he told The Sun. “And I think that's entirely driven by the disincentives right now to pursue a kind of winner-take-all economic toll that has them displacing jobs at the minimum and potentially creating catastrophically dangerous technology.”

El-Sayed also dismissed arguments from AI proponents that the U.S. must lead AI development or else risk the technology falling into the hands of an adversary like China.

“So you're telling me that you're going to race forward into a technology you don't really understand, so that somehow you can have more control over it than they do, except for you don't have control over what you're creating now, and you beating them may, in the interim, create technology we actually can't keep hold of?” he said. “That argument is hard to make.”

entries.title: White House Takes Down ‘Build the Wall’ Game After Tetris’ Lawsuit Threat
entries.summary: The change came after Tetris said it takes “copyright infringement very seriously.”
entries.content:
The White House took down a mass deportation-themed video game called “Build the Wall” from its arcade website this week, just days after The Tetris Company implied its design may represent copyright infringement.

The game was placed on the website as part of a larger rollout of themed games based on President Donald Trump’s agenda. In the game similar to Tetris, players stacked bricks to build a wall to prevent a “zombie border siege.”

Immediately after the game was posted to the White House website, Tetris pushed back, writing that the company was not involved in the creation of the game and takes “copyright infringement very seriously.”

“At Tetris we believe in the power of connection and bringing people together, not dividing them,” the company wrote on X. “To our fans everywhere: we love you, we see you, and we’re grateful to have you in our community.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment from The Washington Sun. Other Trump administration video games, which also resemble popular titles, remain on the White House arcade website.

entries.title: The Military’s Top Officer Says the Pentagon Needs Cash for Weapons Deals
entries.summary: Trump’s ambitious munitions ramp-up hinges on funding Congress has yet to supply.
entries.content:
The U.S. military’s top officer said Wednesday that the Pentagon needs Congress to approve a defense budget as the department negotiates deals with weapons makers to rapidly expand munitions production.

Gen. Dan Caine, the chair of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, stopped short of discussing the Pentagon’s recent munitions agreements specifically. But his comments come as the department is striking ambitious, long-term deals with defense companies whose production goals depend on funding Congress has yet to provide.

Asked about President Donald Trump’s $1.5 trillion budget request for 2027 on stage at the National Defense Industrial Association’s Tech Expo in Washington, D.C., Caine said the military needs money to “procure, field, train and operate” the weapons and other capabilities it’s seeking.

“The $1.5 trillion configuration, that’s a political decision for our policymakers,” Caine said. “But you know we support that and need that capital to make sure that the deals that the department is negotiating with a wide range of not only NDIA members but broader industry members — is essential.”

The stakes are especially high after six months of war with Iran depleted U.S. missile stockpiles that experts have warned are inadequate for a potential conflict with China and will take years to restore. But the administration’s budget is under strain for this year, with next year’s plans facing an uncertain path through Congress.

The Pentagon announced framework agreements last month with Lockheed Martin and General Dynamics that are intended to lead to seven-year purchasing contracts for Patriot Advanced Capability-3 Missile Segment Enhancement and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense missile interceptors.

The agreements are meant to give companies confidence that the government will keep buying weapons for years, incentivizing investments in factories, equipment, workers and suppliers.

Under the agreements, the Pentagon wants to triple Patriot missile production and quadruple production capacity for THAAD missile interceptors. But the department said when it announced the deals that the increases would remain subject to Congress approving the money each year.

Other such deals include the framework agreement with RTX setting annual production goals of more than 1,000 Tomahawk cruise missiles and at least 1,900 advanced medium-range air-to-air missiles. Those framework agreements are not funded contracts either.

The administration’s production push still depends on a Congress that has been struggling to agree on how to finance the defense buildup. The administration made $350 billion of its budget request in reconciliation, a special process that allows legislation to pass the Senate with a simple majority rather than the 60 votes generally needed to overcome a filibuster.

The House in July narrowly approved a fiscal 2027 budget resolution that would allow Republicans to write a roughly $95 billion reconciliation package. It provides instructions for about $60 billion in Pentagon spending, plus $13 billion for intelligence programs — far short of the administration’s request.

That proposal has struggled in the Senate, where there isn’t sufficient Republican support. And Congress, which is in a partisan deadlock over regular appropriations, approved a stopgap this month to keep government funding at current levels through Dec. 11.
entries.author: Joe Gould

entries.title: Pentagon Outsourced Base Services to Local Governments but Can’t Tell if It Saved Money
entries.summary: “They are not required to track that information, and they don’t,” said a government watchdog.
entries.content:
The Pentagon has embraced agreements with state and local governments as a cheaper, faster way to provide mundane services on military bases, such as grass-cutting, trash collection, road repairs and snow removal.

But as the agreements have multiplied, the military has struggled to keep track of how much it is saving over traditional contracting and whether lower worker pay or benefits are contributing to those savings, according to a new Government Accountability Office report shared with The Washington Sun.

The question was central to why Rep. Bobby Scott of Virginia, the top Democrat on the House Education and Workforce Committee, and Rep. Lucy McBath (D-Georgia) asked the GAO in 2024 to investigate the program. They asked auditors to determine whether Pentagon savings came from avoiding wage and benefit minimums required under federal labor laws, and argued — based on the findings — that they do.

“Today’s GAO report shows that not only is the Department of Defense using intergovernmental support agreements to bypass the law, but it is also relying on them,” Scott said. “While the DOD may argue that IGSAs save the government money, it comes at the cost of shortchanging workers of fair wages and decent benefits.”

The military had 316 active intergovernmental support agreements, known as IGSAs, at the end of 2025, according to the GAO report. That number was up dramatically from 45 in 2018. The Army accounted for more than half of these and spent about $355 million on them last year.

Congress authorized IGSAs in 2013, allowing bases to obtain routine services through state, local, and tribal governments. The idea was straightforward: A town that already maintains roads or collects trash may be able to do the same work on a neighboring military base more cheaply than the military can.

But the agreements also operate outside of the Service Contract Act, a 60-year-old labor law that sets local wage and benefit minimums for many workers on federal service contracts. And the military collects little or no information about the labor used under IGSAs, the GAO found.

That leaves the military services unable to definitively say they are saving the Pentagon money and how much of that savings comes from avoiding wage and benefit minimums that would otherwise be required under the law

“There is not good data, and they’re not required to have it,” Thomas Costa, a director on the GAO's Education, Workforce and Income Security team, told The Sun. “They are not required to track that information, and they don’t.”

The Pentagon declined to comment. In the report, the military services generally agreed with the GAO’s recommendations and said they would take steps to improve estimating and verifying savings from IGSAs. The Navy said it would strengthen comparisons of estimated and annual costs, while the Air Force said it would start doing annual reviews comparing actual costs to its estimates.

Auditors tried to determine whether lower labor costs were contributing to Pentagon savings by comparing wages for five public-sector jobs under IGSAs with what similar workers would have been guaranteed if the Service Contract Act applied. But the military collects little information about the workers performing services under IGSAs, making it difficult to draw a definitive conclusion. Of the five jobs examined, three paid minimum rates that were 13% to 19% less, one was about the same and one paid 50% more.

McBath said the findings reinforced her concerns that IGSAs are skirting fair wage laws.

“Working people deserve to be paid what they are owed,” she said. “The Department of Defense should not exploit legal loopholes to pay workers less."

Costa said lower labor costs than what the Pentagon might have paid under fair wage minimums could account for some savings, but they are not necessarily the only explanation. Military officials told the GAO that IGSAs can reduce administrative work and take advantage of efficiencies that come from buying services at a larger scale.“Some of the people working on doing the work are getting paid less than they would under the SCA,” he said. “But there could be other things, such as economies of scale, that factor into that help realize those cost savings.”

Of 21 single-installation agreements the GAO examined, nine used private contractors hired by the local government and not public employees for some or all of the work. In some cases, those contractors also hired subcontractors, adding another layer between the military and the people actually performing the work.

The GAO also found the Navy, Marine Corps and Air Force lacked procedures to verify whether installations’ estimates of IGSA costs and savings were ultimately accurate. The Army told auditors it does track actual costs and savings.The GAO raised similar concerns in 2018 about whether the services were monitoring the benefits of IGSAs. But the numbers are getting harder to track as the military enters an increasing number of agreements that cover multiple services and bases.

“Once you get to that multi-service or multi-installation, the analyses started to get generally worse,” Costa said.

For example, the GAO also examined 402 Army task orders under a nationwide agreement with Sourcewell, a Minnesota government entity that helps public agencies obtain services. Auditors found that 101 either showed no financial benefit or lacked a documented cost comparison.

That meant auditors could not tell whether the deals were good or bad. “The answer is we don’t know,” Costa said.
entries.author: Joe Gould

entries.title: AI Researcher’s Warning Goes Viral as Regulation Stalls in D.C.
entries.summary: Jacob Coxon, a researcher who has worked for several leading AI companies, said the technology could pose an existential threat to humanity.
entries.content:
An artificial intelligence researcher publicly resigned from Anthropic this week over concerns that the technology’s “out of control” progression could lead to widespread disruption that society is unprepared for, a warning that caused a stir online just as a push for more AI regulation has stalled in Washington.

Jacob Coxon’s posts on X circulated widely after he claimed that artificial intelligence companies are not “acting responsibly” with the technology and are instead racing to improve software models with no regard for the existential threat AI poses to the global economy and human civilization. Coxon, who said he worked as a pretraining researcher for three years at both OpenAI and Anthropic, added that AI would soon have the potential to “hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources.”

“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” Coxon wrote. “This is not a marketing stunt. If anything, many executives and senior researchers will couch their phrasing in the press to sound sensible — but I hear the same people express fear privately. No other human activity poses this level of danger.”

Two other leaders in the AI industry echoed Coxon’s concerns following his resignation. Evan Hubinger, a team leader at Anthropic, wrote on X that he believed there was a greater than 10% chance that AI could “kill all humans.” Samuel Marks, another team leader at Anthropic, said “the more senior the employee” at an AI company, “the more concerned they are” about the technology’s power.

OpenAI and Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Coxon’s posts.

Coxon’s warning comes as public scrutiny grows over the rise of AI and the massive investment in data centers needed to power the technology. Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have sought to regulate AI by introducing hundreds of bills, including measures to ban AI chatbots for minors, protect candidates for federal office from deepfakes and establish guardrails for the industry.

The proposals, however, have largely failed to materialize into legislation, leaving some lawmakers worried that Congress is missing a pivotal window to regulate AI.

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) has attempted to introduce several headline-grabbing measures in recent months, including a bill with Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas) to ban “superintelligent” AI entirely and temporarily pause AI development while federal regulation is being discussed.

Rep. Lori Trahan (D-Massachusetts), who introduced a measure in June with Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-California) to establish a federal framework for AI, decided last week to not pursue a party leadership position in order to prioritize AI regulation.

President Donald Trump has embraced the AI industry during his second term, meeting with executives to discuss partnerships with the federal government and dismissing criticism of data centers. Trump has gone as far to say that communities that reject data centers will “end up being backwards and poor.”

“If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place,” Trump wrote on Truth Social Aug. 31, “let Data Reign.”
entries.author: Angie Orellana Hernandez

entries.title: The AP Will Keep Using ‘Lake Ontario’ Despite Trump’s Renaming Effort
entries.summary: The publication said it would refer to the body of water by Trump’s chosen name “Lake America” only “when relevant.”
entries.content:
The Associated Press said it will not refer to Lake Ontario as “Lake America” unless it's deemed “relevant,” despite President Donald Trump’s executive order to rename the body of water.

The AP provides a leading style and formatting guide for journalists, and the publication has faced criticism from the Trump administration for keeping the original names of other landmarks.

“The Associated Press will refer to Lake Ontario by its original name, including the name Trump has chosen when relevant,” AP spokesperson Patrick Maks said in a statement to The Washington Post published Wednesday. “As a global news agency that disseminates news around the world, the AP must ensure that place names and geography are recognizable to broad audiences.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the guidance from the AP.

Trump’s Aug. 27 executive order directed Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to update the Geographic Names Information System to reflect Lake Ontario's name change. The president personally applied pressure on companies like Apple to make the update.

The name change for the body of water that borders both the U.S. and Canada comes as the two countries are locked in an escalating, tit-for-tat trade war.

“The name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America,” Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney wrote last month on X in opposition to Trump’s order.

The AP’s online stylebook points to that dispute: “The border between the United States and Canada runs through Lake Ontario. Trump's order only affects how the United States government refers to the body of water. Canada, as well as other countries and international bodies, are not required to recognize the name change, and Canada has said it will not.”

Since the start of his second administration, Trump changed the names of several bodies of water and land features, and he has recently teased renaming states to display more America-centric titles.

The AP did not follow Trump’s lead to rename the Gulf of Mexico the “Gulf of America.” The publication cited its status as a “global news agency that disseminates news around the world” and asserted that the “body of water has shared borders between the U.S. and Mexico,” so Trump’s executive order would only carry weight in the U.S.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum also did not comply with Trump’s directive to rename the gulf, saying, “For us it is still the Gulf of Mexico, and for the entire world it is still the Gulf of Mexico.”

The AP did abide by Trump’s order to rename Alaska’s Denali as Mount McKinley. Even though lawmakers changed the name in 2015 from McKinley to Denali — which translates to “the tall one” in Alaskan Native languages — Trump pushed to “restore the name of a great president.”

“The area lies solely in the United States and as president, Trump has the authority to change federal geographical names within the country,” the AP wrote in its style guidance on the mountain.
entries.author: Jenna Monnin

entries.title: Minnesota Man Arrested During Trump’s ICE Surge Sent to Guantánamo
entries.summary: Adam Abdullah does not appear to have a criminal record, save for two parking tickets. Now he’s being held in a military prison historically used for terrorism suspects.
entries.content:
Adam Abdullah’s criminal record in Minnesota consists of two parking citations for failing to move his car during snow emergencies. The Somali national paid both tickets — $56 each — in early 2025 within days of the charges, according to Minnesota court records.

But months after a run-in with federal immigration agents in December as part of the Trump administration’s Operation Metro Surge, he’s now sitting in Guantánamo Bay, the infamous military prison historically used for terrorism suspects.

He told Minnesota Public Radio that he had been living legally in the United States with a work permit and a Social Security number since arriving in 2023 as an asylum seeker. He’s one of at least eight Somali nationals currently being housed at the military facility, he said. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement records confirm Abdullah is in custody at Guantánamo Bay’s Camp 6, a detention camp that was repurposed in 2025 to hold migrants.

President Donald Trump has targeted Somalis since his return to office, referring to immigrants as “garbage” and calling Somalia a “hellhole.” In January, the Trump administration ended Temporary Protected Status for Somali nationals.

It remains unclear to Abdullah why he has been detained at Guantánamo Bay. He was told at first that it was a refueling stop on the way to Somalia, and authorities have not provided any further information about his status or why he has remained there for two weeks.

Abdullah said he has also not received an explanation as to why immigration agents stopped his vehicle and detained him in December during the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown in Minnesota.

“When they come to me, and I ask them why you pulled me over, they say, ‘We are immigration, so give me your work permit,’” Abdullah told Minnesota Public Radio, which was the first to report on his detention. “And I asked them, ‘Do you have a warrant, and what’s the reason to pull me over?’ And they say, ‘We don’t need a warrant. We are immigration, and we know you are Adam Abdullah.’”

Abdullah said detainees in Guantánamo Bay have limited access to phone calls and physical activities. He said he’s able to talk to fellow detainees for a few hours during the day.

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security said in a statement Wednesday that the recent flight to Guantánamo Bay included “some of the worst of the worst,” with criminal histories that included allegations of aggravated assaults, weapons offenses, robbery, trespassing, unauthorized use of a vehicle and multiple drug charges.

“President Trump and Secretary Mullin will not allow criminal illegal aliens to terrorize American citizens,” the statement said. “If you come to our country illegally, you could end up in Guantanamo Bay or even another third country.”

DHS did not respond to follow-up questions on Abdullah’s criminal record.

Abdullah’s lawyer did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Trump signed an executive order days after his inauguration to expand Guantánamo Bay’s Migrant Operations Center, a detention facility traditionally used to process migrants intercepted at sea, so it could house “high-priority criminal aliens” prior to deportation.

The first group of detainees arrived in February 2025 as legal challenges quickly mounted to prevent the transfers. The Trump administration continued to send groups to Guantánamo Bay throughout 2025, temporarily housing migrants in tent cities and occasionally sending them back to stateside detention centers.

In May, CBS News reported that six Haitian migrants were being held at Guantánamo Bay. It’s unclear how many migrants are currently being held there.

entries.title: Buying Back Bonds Bigger
entries.content:
Good afternoon, and welcome to The Afternoon Sun, formerly known as Final NOTUS! Read more about our new era as The Washington Sun here, but you can expect the same newsletter and comprehensive coverage of national politics and policy.

THE LATEST

Temporary Protected Status was set to expire for around 200,000 Salvadorans today, but the Trump administration has left their status in question.

  • A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security said that until further notice, “Salvadoran individuals present in the U.S. under TPS retain protection.”
New financial disclosures show that Donald Trump gave several of his close aides — including executive assistant Natalie Harp — a “cash gift” of $45,000 each.

  • The White House said the gifts are “entirely permissible” under the law because they “have nothing to do with any of these individuals’ official government duties.”




THE ADMINISTRATION

A Minnesota man from Somalia with no apparent criminal record — save for two parking tickets — is being held in Guantanamo Bay after being detained by immigration authorities in December. Adam Abdullah told Minnesota Public Radio that he’s one of at least eight Somali nationals being held at the facility.

The White House removed the “Build the Wall” game from its controversial arcade website, just days after the gaming company behind Tetris raised copyright infringement concerns.

The Treasury plans to buy back $6 billion of its own debt as part of its efforts to curb rising bond yields. The amount has tripled from the originally announced $2 billion buyback last month.





THE HILL

The Senate Judiciary Committee will hear testimony from FBI Director Kash Patel on Sept. 15 — the day after senators are set to return from recess.





THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL

Abdul El-Sayed called for a pause on the development of artificial intelligence after viral warnings from several top AI researchers that the technology’s “out of control” progression could lead to widespread disruption and even human extinction.
