entries.title: Maine Gubernatorial Candidate’s Sister Says She’s Voting for His Opponent
entries.summary: Republican Bobby Charles’ sister cited his positions on abortion and education policy in endorsing Democrat Hannah Pingree.
entries.content:
A sibling dispute is now playing out in the governor’s race in Maine, where the sister of Republican nominee Bobby Charles said publicly that she’s supporting his opponent.

Anita Charles, a Lewiston resident, wrote in the Portland Press Herald that she and her brother have never agreed politically but have historically managed their divisions with “civility.” But, she said, an increasing amount of divisive language in her brother’s campaign has motivated her to endorse the Democratic nominee, Hannah Pingree.

Anita Charles wrote in the op-ed that the pair’s mother taught them to respect diversity and treat others with “dignity” while growing up in Maine.

“Those lessons shaped my entire life, as well as my career,” Anita Charles wrote. “They are also the reason I cannot support my brother’s campaign for governor.”

Noting she has been a “lifelong educator,” Anita Charles said she specifically opposes her brother’s proposed policies for Maine’s education system and criticized his comments on the public school system.

Bobby Charles has expressed support for a Republican-backed agenda that increases parental involvement in curriculum and ends diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives in schools. He’s dubbed the program a “no-nonsense” plan.

“I do not believe Bobby has set foot in a public school since he was 18,” Anita Charles wrote. “He has not witnessed what Maine educators do every day, yet he speaks with false certainty about what is wrong with our schools. He’s a D.C. lobbyist who spent more than 30 years in Washington.”

She also noted her brother’s relationship with disgraced former House Speaker Dennis Hastert, who admitted to sexually abusing teenage boys and covering up the abuse. Anita Charles wrote that she was the victim of sexual violence by an adult as a child, a fact she said her brother has known for more than 50 years.

She added that her brother’s position on abortion is also difficult for her to accept as a victim of sexual assault. Bobby Charles has called himself “unapologetically pro-life.”

“Maine deserves leadership rooted in empathy, dignity, intellectual honesty and respect for every person who calls this state home,” Anita Charles wrote. “That person is not Bobby. That is why I cannot, in good conscience, support my brother’s campaign for governor. I’m casting my vote for Hannah Pingree.”

Bobby Charles told local media Wednesday that he loves his sister and called for a broader discussion over their disagreements on various policy issues including education, public safety and abortion, News Center Maine reported.

The candidate grew emotional while speaking about his sister’s assault, clarifying his views on abortion.

"I don't believe in late-term abortion, he said. “I don't think the public should be paying for abortions, but it's not my big issue. And to be honest, that kind of a situation is so horrifying that, of course, there are exceptions.”

A poll commissioned by the Portland Press Herald and The New York Times and conducted by Siena Research in June found that Pingree had a sizable lead over Charles, with 50% of voters saying they’d vote for her to Charles’ 36%.

Bobby Charles’ campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment from The Washington Sun.

entries.title: Alexandria Leaders Want to Get Rid of the City’s Flock Cameras
entries.summary: Mayor Alyia Gaskins and multiple City Council members called for potential removal of Flock license-plate readers.
entries.content:
The city of Alexandria wants to get rid of its Flock automated license-plate-reading cameras amid nationwide pushback against the company for reported misuse of its data.

Mayor Alyia Gaskins and multiple City Council members called for review and potential removal of Flock-brand cameras over concerns of potential invasions of privacy. Other cities across the country have reported abuse, such as officials using the license-plate readers to stalk ex-partners and track people's movements unrelated to any crime.

The Institute for Justice, a nonprofit law firm based in Arlington, has documented more than 200 alleged instances of misuse across the U.S. since 2018. There are also concerns the information could be shared with Immigration and Customs Enforcement to unlawfully track immigrants.

“I do not think there is a role for Flock in this community,” Gaskins said Tuesday at a City Council meeting. “There is still a role for technology … but there is agreement that we need to be moving away from the current vendor that we have.”

Getting rid of Flock cameras doesn’t necessarily mean the city will scrap license-plate cameras altogether, but there is a consensus among leaders that the city should move forward with a different vendor if it chooses to keep using the technology.

The Alexandria Police Department has 61 Flock cameras, the first of which were installed in 2023. There may be more automated license cameras in city limits, but those are maintained by other entities such as private land owners or education institutions. City cameras delete data after 21 days unless associated with an active investigation.

In the past month, the city has run 327 searches in its Flock database, according to a newly published online portal. The city has data-sharing agreements with 161 other jurisdictions within Virginia, but Alexandria Police Chief Tarrick McGuire said at Tuesday’s meeting that no agencies outside of the commonwealth, including federal agencies like ICE, are able to access the city’s cameras.

McGuire said internal audits show zero instances of misuse within the department, but reporting from the Alexandria Times showed the police had documented 56, most of which stemmed from officers not giving proper explanations as to why a search was run. McGuire said the Police Department has multiple safeguards in place to prevent misuse of the Flock system, such as internal auditing and restricting access to trained personnel.

“As leaders, our responsibility is not to choose between public safety and civil liberties. Our responsibility is to ensure that both are protected,” he said Tuesday. “The Constitution … requires us to govern in a way that safeguards the rights of individuals while protecting all persons in our communities.”

The city can terminate its contract with Flock at any time. No official action or proposal to withdraw has been taken. The city is in talks to secure an independent auditor for the system, which City Manager James Parajon said should be finalized in about a week.

entries.title: Trump Says Oil Prices Will Remain High Until After the Midterms
entries.summary: The president said gas prices will be "tumbling downward" after the election.
entries.content:
By AAMER MADHANI

President Donald Trump said Wednesday that oil prices that have surged because of the Iran war likely won’t come down until after U.S. midterm elections.

Oil prices on Wednesday jumped more than 3%, pushing international Brent crude past the $100 threshold for the first time since July as salvos between the U.S. and Iran escalated.

“Right after the election, oil prices are going to be tumbling downward,” Trump said. “I think it’s going to take a little bit longer than the midterm.”

Trump, in an exchange with reporters before traveling to Dallas for the midterm Republican convention, added that he believes Iran will finally relent after the pivotal elections are held in the U.S.

“I think the war’s going to end immediately after the election because they can’t hold out any longer,” Trump said.

The president at the outset of the war said it would last a matter of weeks. The conflict is now in its seventh month. The U.S.-Israel war against Iran has led to a dramatic slowdown of Gulf oil moving through the Strait of Hormuz, which about 20% of the world’s petroleum passed through prior to the conflict.

The comments were a striking acknowledgment from Trump about the conflict as his Republican administration faces mounting pressure to address high gas prices as the war in Iran grinds on with no conclusion in sight.

Trump last week downplayed the conflict as “small potatoes" even as Republicans expressed concern the war will loom large with voters left navigating elevated gas prices and higher inflation.

The U.S. has tapped its strategic petroleum reserves, which in early August fell below 300 million barrels, down by more than 100 million barrels since the start of 2026.

Trump's prediction that the war won't be wrapped up until after Nov. 3 comes after Vice President JD Vance last week steered clear of predicting that the conflict would be over by the midterm elections, in which Republicans are trying to hang on to their narrow majorities in Congress.

Vance told reporters he didn’t want to set “artificial timelines” for the war's end.

“But when you ask, ‘When will this end?’ You’re asking me a question like, ‘When will the Iranians stop shooting at ships?’” Vance said. “I think the reality is, I don’t know the answer to that question. You would have to ask the Iranians.”

U.S. benchmark crude on Wednesday gained 2.4%, pushing the price to $95.25 a barrel, and U.S. gasoline prices rose sharply overnight.

The average price for a gallon of regular gasoline ticked up 7 cents overnight t o hit $4.22, now more than a dollar above what it cost at this point last year, according to AAA.

Diesel prices, which can have an outsize impact on consumers because it is used in shipping and production, hit an all-time high Friday and have continued to climb since. The average price per gallon rose to $5.94 overnight, up 9 cents from Friday.

Jet fuel has become so expensive that U.S. and international carriers have cut flights while raising fares and fees.

Markets reacted after the U.S. military reported striking five Iranian tankers in response to attempted missile attacks on a Navy warship and after attacks by an Iranian-backed Houthi rebel group ignited fires at oil facilities in Saudi Arabia.
___

AP writer Cathy Bussewitz contributed reporting.

entries.title: The White House Called Fox News’ CEO to Complain About Bartiromo Firing
entries.summary: Administration officials conveyed to the network that the firing was “totally unacceptable,” White House trade adviser Peter Navarro said.
entries.content:
A top adviser to President Donald Trump said this week that unnamed White House officials called Fox News CEO Suzanne Scott to complain following the network’s ouster of longtime personality Maria Bartiromo.

It’s the latest twist in a long and complicated relationship between the Trump-era White House and Fox News, and comes after reports suggested Bartiromo’s ouster was a result of her decision to share newsroom communications about coverage with the White House.

Peter Navarro, Trump’s senior counselor for trade and manufacturing, made the claim during an appearance Tuesday on Newsmax’s “Greg Kelly Reports.” He also claimed the incident was evidence that Fox News was suppressing pro-Trump coverage and had abandoned its role as a conservative agenda-setter.

“Suffice it to say that Suzanne Scott got a call, and basically the White House let her know that that kind of thing is totally unacceptable,” Navarro said.

He later added: “The bigger story here is, forget about anybody thinking that Fox is a conservative network that’s friendly to MAGA, that’s friendly to Trump.”

Navarro’s comments came days after Fox announced that Bartiromo was no longer with the company after more than 12 years there. The network called her departure a “business decision” but did not provide a specific reason.

In an op-ed published Tuesday, Navarro said Bartiromo had planned to interview him about Trump’s July 16 speech, in which the president discussed debunked allegations of Chinese interference in the 2020 election. Navarro said Bartiromo later sent him internal guidance telling Fox Business staff not to promote the speech or discuss the 2020 election, which he passed along to other White House officials. Bartiromo’s disclosure of internal coverage decisions ultimately led to her firing, the media newsletter Status reported.

Bartiromo’s attorney, Bryan Freedman, has disputed that she was fired, saying reports that she was no longer a Fox employee were “absolutely and unequivocally false.”

Navarro nevertheless blamed Scott for what he described as a broader effort to keep Trump-focused coverage within limits.

“Suzanne Scott is the enforcer,” Navarro said on Newsmax, arguing that Fox will give its audience conservative programming while avoiding some of the issues most important to Trump and his supporters.

Fox has faced costly legal battles over its coverage of the 2020 election, and Bartiromo was among the Fox personalities named in several lawsuits alleging the network promoted false claims about voting-machine companies. Fox settled Dominion Voting Systems’ lawsuit for $787.5 million in 2023, while a separate Smartmatic case remains pending.

Trump has defended Bartiromo since her departure, calling her a “total professional” and “true warrior.”

Navarro has gone further, portraying Bartiromo’s exit as evidence that Fox is pulling back from some of the issues that have defined Trump’s relationship with the network.

“The muzzling of Maria Bartiromo by Fox News Media Chief Executive Suzanne Scott should be a wake-up call to every Fox viewer who believes the network is pro-Trump and pro-MAGA,” he wrote.

entries.title: Frances Tiafoe, the DMV’s Favorite Tennis Star, Is Leveling Up
entries.summary: Chasing his first major title, the College Park native will face Ben Shelton in the U.S. Open semi.
entries.content:
Frances Tiafoe has earned another shot at superstardom. The 28-year-old tennis star, a Maryland native, will face Ben Shelton on Friday in a highly anticipated U.S. Open semifinal. A win would put him one step away from his first major title and a chance to be the first American man to win the U.S. Open singles bracket since 2003.

Tiafoe advanced to the semifinals after a thrilling five-set defeat of 22-year-old American Alex Michelsen on Tuesday. Down two sets early, he rallied for a 5-7, 3-6, 7-5, 6-3, 7-6 (10-6) win.

Tiafoe and Michelsen had an emotional hug at the end of the match that quickly went viral.

“I really like Alex. I really, really do, and I just wanted to come up there and just dap him up,” Tiafoe said. “I didn’t think it was going to be as long as it was, but I understand the moment. He was definitely crying on my shoulders. Yeah, we just had some words for each other, and that was it.”

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Later — much later — in the day’s slate, Shelton upset Carlos Alcaraz to set a semifinal meeting.

The last time Shelton and Tiafoe faced off was at the D.C. Open in July 2025. Shelton defeated Tiafoe in straight sets. Shelton owns a 3-1 record in their lifetime series.

Fellow Maryland native and Sportscenter host Scott Van Pelt tweeted in support of Tiafoe after Tuesday’s win, as did the University of Maryland’s official athletic account. Tiafoe, who was born and raised near College Park, has attended many Terps games over the years.

Frances Tiafoe AP - 26251836298808 (5823x3882, AR: 1.50)
Tiafoe’s story is well known by now. His parents immigrated to the U.S. from Sierra Leone to escape the country’s civil war, and his father, Frances Sr., worked construction on the Junior Tennis Champions Center in College Park. Frances Sr. lived out of the tennis center for more than a decade and Tiafoe, and his twin brother, Franklin, learned to play the sport in their spare time.

Eventually, Tiafoe moved to Florida to play at the USTA National Training Center while Franklin stayed in Maryland and attended DeMatha. Frances made his ATP Tour debut at 16.

The 28-year-old’s semifinal run matches the longest of his career. Tiafoe has never won a Grand Slam event, but has made the U.S. Open semifinals twice before, his deepest runs at any major.

Andy Roddick was the last American man to win the U.S. Open, in 2003. Roddick reached the men’s final again in 2006, but no American repeated that feat until 2024, when Taylor Fritz beat Tiafoe in the semi before falling to champion Jannik Sinner.

According to ESPN, the winner of Shelton and Tiafoe’s semifinal will also be the first Black American to reach the U.S. Open men’s final since Arthur Ashe in 1972 and the first to reach any major final since MaliVai Washington in 1996 at Wimbledon.

But Tiafoe likely won’t be the only beloved D.C. sports figure at Flushing Meadows on Friday: Trinity Rodman, Shelton’s girlfriend, can often be found in the crowd at his matches.

entries.title: El Salvador TPS Holders ‘Retain Protection’ Pending a DHS Decision on Their Fate
entries.summary: The designation was set to expire on Wednesday, leaving around 200,000 in a legal limbo.
entries.content:
The Trump administration has yet to make a decision on the fate of around 200,000 Salvadorans living in the United States under Temporary Protected Status, even though the designation was set to expire today.

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security said that until a further announcement is made, “Salvadoran individuals present in the U.S. under TPS retain protection.” Some Salvadorans with TPS protections have had it for decades. Salvadorans were the first immigrants granted TPS in 1990 following the nation’s civil war. They again received the protection in 2001 after earthquakes rocked the small country, and the designation has been renewed every time it has been up for reconsideration since.

Under TPS, immigrants have no direct mechanism through which to obtain permanent legal status. The designation allows immigrants protection from deportation and the ability to legally work in the United States.

Under President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, DHS has eliminated protections for immigrants from 14 countries, roughly 1.3 million people, including for immigrants from Haiti, Syria and Venezuela. Lebanon, Ukraine and Sudan are the last three countries with TPS, in addition to El Salvador, and their designation is up for renewal in the coming months.

Dulce Guzmán, the executive director of the nonprofit coalition Alianza Americas, said Salvadoran TPS holders have been “living in limbo” as they await a decision from the Trump administration. The lack of a formal decision on Wednesday has only created more uncertainty for immigrants who are supposedly protected by the announcement today.

“Without having a formal announcement or document that TPS holders can provide to their employers or the DMV, it really is just not a significant enough protection for people,” Guzmán said, adding that these TPS holders would have nothing to show immigration agents if they are stopped or detained.

In June, the Supreme Court allowed the Trump administration to end the legal protections for immigrants fleeing from Haiti and Syria, overturning lower court orders and opening the way for the complete dismantling of the program.

DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin is required to give a 60-day notice of intention to terminate status before it ends, although with previous countries that has not been the case. If DHS does not make a decision on a TPS designation, it is automatically extended for another six months.

“It’s really important for communities to hear directly from the administration through the formal process that the law has established to let communities know you know how to prepare and how to navigate this uncertainty,” Guzmán said. “This does not only affect the TPS holders themselves, but it also affects their children, their families, the employers that depend on their labor and local economy.”

This article has been updated with comments from Dulce Guzmán.

entries.title: Sen. Tim Scott Says Democratic Senate Candidates ‘Hate’ American Culture
entries.summary: The South Carolina Republican went down the list of Democratic candidates in key Senate races, accusing them of being “dangerous, radical and frankly weird.”
entries.content:
Sen. Tim Scott accused Democratic Senate candidates of being “dangerous, radical and frankly weird” and said they “hate what it means to be American” during a speech Wednesday at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas.

Scott, of South Carolina, who chairs the National Republican Senatorial Committee, used his speech to attack Democratic candidates in several key Senate races, arguing that Republicans must keep their majority to advance President Donald Trump’s agenda.

“They hate our culture,” Scott said to cheers from the crowd. “They hate what it means to be American.”

Scott singled out candidates including James Talarico in Texas, Sen. Jon Ossoff in Georgia, Sherrod Brown in Ohio, Roy Cooper in North Carolina, Troy Jackson in Maine, Josh Turek in Iowa, Chris Pappas in New Hampshire, Mary Peltola in Alaska and Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan.

His attacks focused heavily on cultural issues.

Scott went after Talarico over his views on gender and religion, saying the candidate “claims there are six genders” and “believes God is non-binary.” Talarico is running for Senate in a race Republicans have made a major target.

Scott accused Ossoff of supporting allowing boys to play girls’ sports and criticized El-Sayed over comments Scott attributed to him criticizing football, Fourth of July fireworks and Israel.

“But worst of all, Abdul El-Sayed panders with terrorists,” Scott said, without offering evidence.

Scott’s speech came as Republicans gathered in Dallas for the party’s first-ever midterm convention, a two-day event designed to rally support for GOP candidates ahead of the November elections.

Scott closed by urging Republicans to unite behind Trump and defend the GOP’s Senate majority.

“This is a battle for the heart of our nation,” Scott said. “We will not back down. We will not grow weary.”

entries.title: Missouri Redistricting Case Reaches Supreme Court — Again
entries.summary: The legal battle is now playing out in four courts less than two months before the midterms.
entries.content:
The question of which congressional map Missouri should use in the midterms is back before the U.S. Supreme Court.

The legal tussle over whether to use a 2022 map or one redrawn to favor Republicans now spans four courts and is before the nation’s high court for the second time.

On Wednesday, the citizens group People Not Politicians and its executive director, Richard Von Glahn, asked the Supreme Court to overturn a lower court-issued order from Tuesday night that mandated Missouri use a map drawn by Republicans in 2025 that splits up one of two Democratic districts.

That legal turn came after the Missouri Supreme Court ruled that Denny Hoskins, the secretary of state, must use the 2022 map for the midterms.

“The Secretary has made clear that every hour the [temporary restraining order] remains in force, election officials will continue to implement a congressional map that Missouri’s highest court has held is not and never has been law,” the lawyers for People Not Politicians wrote seeking a U.S. Supreme Court intervention.

The case goes through Justice Brett Kavanaugh, the Trump appointee who deals with emergency cases relating to Missouri.

Hoskins is also preparing to defend himself Thursday morning before the Missouri Supreme Court, which is threatening to hold him in contempt for giving conflicting orders as to what map election officials should use.

Missouri was one of the first states to redistrict after President Donald Trump called on Republican state lawmakers to redraw congressional maps to boost their chances this cycle.

Missouri’s state Legislature split up Kansas City in three ways, all but eliminating Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver’s seat.

People Not Politicians gathered more than double the amount of signatures necessary to force a referendum on the new Republican-friendly map.

Hoskins waited until the last possible day to reject the petition — the same day of the state’s primary elections. That move prompted a lawsuit by the citizens group that eventually reached the U.S. Supreme Court, which let stand Missouri’s high court ruling.

entries.title: Fetterman Bashes ‘Socialism’ in Surprise GOP Convention Appearance
entries.summary: The Pennsylvania Democrat spoke to the convention via video in a move that adds more wrinkles to his relationship with his party.
entries.content:
Sen. John Fetterman staged a surprise appearance at the Republican convention Wednesday night in a video criticizing democratic socialists and praising his fellow Pennsylvania senator, Republican Dave McCormick.

“I’m always going to stand with America. I’m always going to reject the extremes and socialism and that anti-American way of life,” Fetterman, a Democrat, said.

Fetterman promised to work with President Donald Trump to defend the Pennsylvania steel industry.

Questions have swirled for months over the senator’s future party affiliation, especially with Democrats now competing to win enough seats to take control of the Senate. In July, Fetterman said he would switch parties if Democrats became “the anti-Israel party.” Fetterman has backed Republicans in recent Iran war powers votes and, in conservative media appearances, has increasingly supported Trump-led policies.

Fetterman wrote in a Washington Post op-ed in May that he is an “an independent voice that works with the other side to deliver for Pennsylvanians” with “no plans” to leave the Democratic Party.

“Plus,” he wrote, “I’d be a terrible Republican who still votes overwhelmingly with Democrats.”

Fetterman’s Wednesday video served as an introduction for McCormick's speech at the Dallas gathering. Axios reported that McCormick helped arrange the appearance. In his video, Fetterman fell short of announcing a party switch.

“He’s in a different party, but I’m proud to count him as my great friend,” Fetterman said.

Pennsylvania state Sen. Scott Martin, who watched the video from the convention floor in Dallas, told The Washington Sun that there was “symbolism” in Fetterman’s appearance.

“I think it’s the willingness to work hand-in-hand for two U.S. senators to focus on different issues that greatly impact Pennsylvanians,” he said in an interview. He wouldn’t go much further in speculating about Fetterman’s future.

“I know there's a lot swirling on in Democratic Party politics related to him, and they'll obviously deal with that,” Martin said. “But as long as he's a U.S. senator willing to work hand-in-hand on the issues that are really important to help a Pennsylvania that desperately needs to grow economically and demographically, I'll take them working together.”

He did say if Fetterman ever switched parties, he believed his party would welcome him.

The Democratic senator’s appearance comes less than a week after he was denounced by many in his party for neglecting his senatorial duties.

The senator’s term ends in 2028, and he has not confirmed whether he will seek reelection.

entries.title: Blanche Departs From DOJ Norms With a Speech at Republican Convention
entries.summary: The Justice Department said the attorney general’s appearance is in his “personal capacity” and had been “approved by ethics.”
entries.content:
Attorney General Todd Blanche is set to speak Wednesday night at the most partisan of events — the Republican Party’s midterm convention — weeks after a Senate confirmation fight that focused largely on his potential to politicize the Department of Justice.

Blanche is scheduled to take the stage between 7 p.m. and 8 p.m. ET at what has been billed as a “Trump-a-palooza.” He is appearing on a roster of speakers that includes numerous congressional candidates, other administration officials and President Donald Trump himself.

His planned remarks at the arena in Dallas represent a sharp departure from Justice Department norms and would have been barred by department policy had Trump administration officials not quietly changed the rules last year, according to former DOJ officials.

Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee criticized the move, accusing Blanche of violating federal law — ostensibly the Hatch Act, which restricts the political activities of federal employees. “Amazing how far the DOJ has fallen,” the committee’s Democrats said on social media.

In response, the Justice Department said Blanche was appearing in his “personal capacity,” that his appearance was legal and had been “approved by ethics.”

Blanche already broke with DOJ tradition last month when he spoke at a political rally in New York and praised a Republican candidate for governor.

His speech Wednesday is without modern precedent. In 1964, then-Attorney General Robert F. Kennedy spoke at the Democratic National Convention, but to pay tribute to his late brother, former President John F. Kennedy, who was assassinated the previous November.

Attorneys general and other senior law-enforcement leaders generally don’t participate in overtly political events to avoid the appearance of using the immense weight of the Justice Department to tip the balance in an election, former DOJ officials said.

“The idea that Todd Blanche could speak at this type of event and people not take it as an official speech of his office is pure fiction,” said Joseph Tirrell, a former DOJ senior ethics official. “And he could very well ruin the fiction altogether if he says anything that makes clear he’s speaking in his official capacity, or if he starts talking about election enforcement. If he mentions where he works, if he mentions activities or programs by the Department of Justice, even if he says good things about protecting elections and making sure they’re as free and fair, that’s crossing the line.”

Blanche's close alignment with Trump, including his role as the president's former criminal defense lawyer, came up repeatedly in his confirmation hearing over the summer. Democrats pressed him on whether he could be trusted to maintain the Justice Department's historic independence from the White House.

During the proceeding, Blanche fumbled a softball question on the issue from Sen. John Kennedy (R-Louisiana), saying of Trump, "I'm his lawyer," before correcting himself to say he “was his lawyer, and now I’m the deputy attorney general.” In a “Meet the Press” interview after his confirmation, Blanche refused to say he’d act independently from the White House.

The Hatch Act limits the political activities of two groups of federal employees: those known as “less restricted” and “further restricted.”

The “less restricted” group includes most career employees in the executive branch, as well as some political appointees, who are permitted to advocate for candidates or political organizations as long as they don’t do so in their official capacity.

The “further restricted” group covers officials in leadership positions. This includes national security leaders and others directly involved in law enforcement, as well as Federal Election Commission officials and other agency heads, who must adhere to much tighter limits.

Long-standing DOJ policy considered all political appointees in the department — even those who weren’t Senate-confirmed — as falling into the latter category. The policy was written more than 20 years ago and reauthorized with minor tweaks across Republican and Democratic administrations.

“They basically can vote, they can donate money, they can put campaign signs in their yard, and that’s really about it,” said Tirrell, who served as the Department of Justice’s ethics director until then-Attorney General Pam Bondi fired him last summer. “They can speak about a candidate in personal capacity, but they can’t do it in coordination with a campaign.”

Officials in the DOJ’s upper echelons were discouraged from attending even relatively small events to avoid the appearance of bringing the department’s imprimatur to a political campaign. Tirrell said he advised DOJ officials in prior administrations not to speak at local holiday events because others on the speaker docket were elected officials running for office. Even that presented an ethical concern, he said.

“That’s how far away from crossing the boundary we tried to keep people,” Tirrell said. “Even appearing on stage by a podium with a candidate for office was considered too fine a line. Even during the first Trump administration, this is the advice that was provided and this is the advice that was heeded, because they hadn’t taken the step to rescind that rule.”

Stacey Young, a former longtime Justice Department trial attorney who now heads the DOJ alum network Justice Connection, said DOJ leaders from both parties had long held political appointees to a high standard when it came to keeping partisan politics out of government.

“The American people must trust that the department's legal judgments are impartial and insulated from politics,” she said in a statement. “The Attorney General knows this, yet sees no problem speaking at political rallies in New York and now at the RNC. These actions are extremely damaging to the department he leads, whether they comply with the letter of DOJ's recently weakened policy or not.”

Former Attorney General Eric Holder called Blanche’s speech "disgraceful" in brief comments to NewsNation on Tuesday. “Attorneys general don’t talk about political things,” Holder said. “He shouldn’t be there.”

entries.title: ICE Opens a Tip Line to Report Undocumented Truck Drivers
entries.summary: DHS has pushed to get noncitizen commercial drivers off the road, despite data indicating they comprise a small number of fatal trucking accidents.
entries.content:
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin launched a new tip line Wednesday for reporting individuals who have fraudulently applied for a commercial driver’s license.

The new tip line, run by Immigration and Customs Enforcement, asks Americans to report any truck driver they suspect of being undocumented. It’s the latest move in the Trump administration’s crackdown on fraudulent commercial driver’s license holders following a number of high-profile crashes involving foreign-born drivers.

“Too many American lives have been lost or permanently changed because illegal aliens who have no business being on our roads have been granted CDLs,” Mullin said.

In March, some 200,000 truck drivers began losing their commercial licenses after the Department of Homeland Security announced that asylum seekers, refugees and recipients of the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program would no longer be eligible to obtain or renew CDLs, which are required to operate buses, semitrucks and tractor-trailers.

And though Homeland Security pointed to a series of fatal accidents around the country, federal data does not indicate that noncitizen commercial drivers cause a disproportionate share of fatal crashes, and the Transportation Department has previously said there is not enough data to establish a relationship between immigrant truckers and fatal crashes.

At a March congressional hearing, Rep. Josh Brecheen (R-Oklahoma) said at least 17 of a total 5,134 fatal crashes in 2025 involved undocumented immigrants driving commercial vehicles.

A social media post from DHS featuring a 30-second animation made in the style of a vintage cartoon called “Fraud Roadsters” garnered thousands of views on X, with many republishing the video and calling for action.

“I'm going to drive on I-35 tomorrow for however long it takes to find and report at least 10 foreigners,” one user said on X.

“REPORT EVERYONE THAT LOOKS LIKE THEY’RE NOT AN AMERICAN,” wrote another.

Several civil rights groups have opposed the crackdown, aiming to reverse what they call discriminatory license cancellations. They have accused the Trump administration of using isolated crashes to portray immigrant drivers broadly as a safety threat and drumming up profiling incidents of immigrant drivers.

In a July court filing, a coalition that included the Sikh Coalition, the Asian Law Caucus, United Sikhs, Stop AAPI Hate and Truckers Movement for Justice said the administration was using immigration status as a proxy for safety. The groups asserted that the Trump administration’s policy has exposed immigrant drivers to a greater number of commercial-vehicle inspections as “a pretext for immigration arrests.”

entries.title: Trump Says He’d ‘Consider’ Pardoning Michael Cohen
entries.summary: The president and Cohen appear to be on a path to reconciliation after their relationship publicly imploded at the end of Trump’s first term.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump said he would “consider” a pardon for his former fixer turned foe, Michael Cohen.

Asked if he planned to pardon his former attorney, Trump told reporters Wednesday he had “never been asked that question” and reiterated that he believed Cohen had recanted his testimony in the New York fraud case against him.

“If everything is checking out, it's something I would consider,” Trump said before departing for the GOP midterm convention in Dallas. “What they did to Michael Cohen was a disgrace. They forced him to say things that he didn't want to say and that he didn't believe.”

Trump added that he appreciated that “although late, he came out and rectified the situation.”

The relationship between Trump and his former attorney soured after the FBI raided Cohen’s home and office in 2018. A judge sentenced Cohen to three years in federal prison in November of that year in connection with a hush money scheme, while Trump remained in the Oval Office.

Trump and Cohen seem to have reconciled of late; the president appeared on his former attorney’s radio show last month. On Sept. 4, Trump claimed Cohen “fully recanted his testimony” — though Cohen has not made any statements formally retracting specific claims he made in the legal or congressional record.

Cohen and Trump have two decades of history between them, and it now appears that the president’s former fixer is trying to get back in Trump’s good graces. Washington Sun reporters spotted Cohen on Wednesday at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas.

Trump has previously called Cohen a “convicted liar, felon and jailbird” after he turned against him during his congressional testimony and later in Trump’s criminal trial.

Cohen said he was “ashamed that [he] chose to take part in concealing Mr. Trump’s illicit acts” and called the president a “racist,” a “con man” and a “cheat,” during his testimony before Congress in 2019.

Cohen was also the star witness during Trump’s criminal trial in 2024 on hush money payments made to two women who claimed to have had sex with Trump. Cohen said that Trump directed him to “take care of it” and knew about the $130,000 payment Cohen made to adult film star Stormy Daniels.

entries.title: States Say Compliance With USPS Ballot Rule Would Take ‘Herculean’ Effort
entries.summary: In a Supreme Court filing, they say damage to the election outweighs the government’s fears about the possibility of voter fraud.
entries.content:
Nearly half the states and voting rights groups are warning the Supreme Court that it might be impossible to comply with a new U.S. Postal Service rule for the midterm elections.

Amid the Trump administration’s legal push to implement the rule, new filings on Wednesday from 23 states, the District of Columbia and voting groups stressed that the USPS has not developed key parts of the system that would heap additional work on state election officials.

“The efforts that state and local elections officials would have to undertake to even begin an attempt at compliance are herculean,” the filing from the states says.

“Each step of this process is fraught with an extreme risk of error,” it continues. “And even if state and local officials were somehow able to implement the new rule perfectly, there is a high risk of technical breakdown, ineptitude, and delay on the part of USPS.”

The Trump administration has asked the justices to lift a lower court decision that has blocked key parts of the USPS rule through Election Day, Nov. 3. It is the latest development in a legal clash that has already been to the Supreme Court once, and now puts the issue back before the justices.

The states argue the harms to the election outweigh the government’s fears about the possibility of voter fraud. In the published rule, the USPS wrote that it has the legal authority to carry out the rule, “whether or not voter fraud is common or uncommon.”

That, the filing says, unravels the administration’s argument that there will be “irreparable harm” if the courts don’t allow the USPS to enforce the rule.

With the midterm elections just weeks away, the states and voting groups emphasize that complying with new rules on how to vote by mail could disenfranchise millions of voters.

That includes an approval process for ballot envelopes — which many states have already purchased for their primaries and may have to return — and upgrading systems to comply with a new Intelligent Mail barcode, or IMb, for every ballot.

For California, that requirement would mean updating the systems in all 58 counties. California’s statewide voter-registration system “is not currently equipped to receive IMb information for individual voters from county election management systems,” the state’s filing says, and those county systems are not prepared “to store and transmit” IMb information.

The process also requires uploading the information of every eligible voter into the USPS Ballot Portal. That database is untested and completely new to election officials, who will need to train staff on how it’s used, the states told the justices.

North Carolina has already begun to mail out ballots, and a handful of other states are mailing ballots in September.

Wisconsin, which has to send out ballots by Sept. 17, added in the filing that it would be impossible for it to comply.

“Wisconsin’s envelopes could only become mailable under the new USPS rule if the State’s elections officers could ‘print and hand-affix stickers with the Rule-compliant IMb codes on’ each envelope,” the filing said. “But that labor-intensive solution invites errors that risk disenfranchising voters.”

Voting rights groups added that the changes this close to an election would disenfranchise eligible voters, particularly those who “must vote by mail due to age, disabilities, language-assistance needs, college attendance, residence in rural areas, and other reasons.”

The USPS has made it clear that if a batch of ballots has errors, which could include thousands of ballots, the ballots will not be delivered. With no margin for error but a lack of safeguards for states that would have to use new technology and systems, voting rights groups expressed little confidence that the new rules would not disrupt the voting process.

“And even if compliance were possible, the members would still face substantial risk of disenfranchisement, given the high likelihood that millions of ballots will be rejected from the Rule’s rushed implementation and zero-tolerance verification regime,” voting rights groups said in the filing. “Disenfranchisement is not only ‘predictable,’ it is ‘Unavoidable.’”

entries.title: Democrats in Congress Plan to Investigate AI Companies
entries.summary: Top House Oversight Democrat vows investigations while others seek the creation of a select committee.
entries.content:
DALLAS — Democrats in Congress are planning to investigate artificial intelligence companies if they win the majority in November — plans that emerged after a former Anthropic researcher said AI technology would eventually end humanity, The Washington Sun has learned.

“There’s going to be a lot of interest from the House Democratic Caucus to immediately begin this process,” Rep. Robert Garcia (D-California), the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, said in an interview Wednesday. “Anytime you have folks talking about AI moving towards extinction of human life, I think that's got to rise to the top of priorities for us in Congress.”

In the Senate, Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Arizona) sent a letter to Majority Leader John Thune and Minority Leader Chuck Schumer urging them to create a bipartisan select committee on AI at the beginning of next Congress to conduct hearings and investigations.

“A dedicated, bipartisan committee with the … staff, authorities, and access to classified and technical briefings necessary to conduct sustained oversight is the response this moment requires,” Gallego wrote in the letter, which was shared first with The Sun.

The plans emerged after Jacob Coxon, a former researcher for Anthropic and OpenAI, announced on X he resigned from Anthropic over concerns that “neither company is acting responsibly” with the technology and are racing to improve software models with no regard for the existential threat AI poses to the global economy and human civilization.

“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt. If anything, many executives and senior researchers will couch their phrasing in the press to sound sensible — but I hear the same people express fear privately. No other human activity poses this level of danger,” Coxon said.

Evan Hubinger, a current researcher working for Anthropic, concurred with Coxon: “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade,” he said on X.

“I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to,” Hubinger added.

Garcia, who is likely to become Oversight chair if Democrats win the House in November, told The Sun he found Coxon’s claims “disturbing” and said Congress “has to move quickly.” Garcia is in Dallas doing Democratic counterprogramming while Republicans are gathered in the city for their midterm convention.

Gallego told Senate leadership that “Congress's current committee structure is not built” to police a rapidly developing technology that evolves every few months.

“Jurisdiction over AI is scattered across multiple Senate committees, each with a focused lens but none with the full picture,” the senator from Arizona wrote.

A select committee on AI, Gallego said, would give Congress “a dedicated venue for direct, sustained engagement with industry, academia, national security officials, and labor.”

“Congress should not wait for a catastrophic failure, widespread economic disruption, or a national security crisis before building the institutional capacity necessary to understand and respond to this technology,” he added.

House Democratic leadership is reportedly considering creating a select committee on AI, Politico reported, and other Democrats have called for a pause on AI development.

“There has to be public hearings; and we can get answers not just from those that are building this AI right now, but also the CEOs who are leading these companies,” Garcia said.

Anthropic and OpenAI did not immediately respond to The Washington Sun’s requests for comment.

entries.title: Bernie Sanders Plans AI Briefing for Fellow Senators
entries.summary: The briefing comes as Sanders escalates his push for Congress to slow down the industry.
entries.content:
Sen. Bernie Sanders is bringing his campaign to slow the development of artificial intelligence to his Senate colleagues, organizing a bipartisan briefing for next week that will feature some of the country’s leading AI researchers.

Sanders sent a “dear colleague” letter to senators urging them to attend the Sept. 16 briefing, which will focus on the potential risks posed by increasingly powerful AI systems, according to Axios, which first reported the letter.

“Congress needs SERIOUS discussions about this issue,” Sanders wrote. “That is why I will be convening a private briefing with some of the leading experts in the world to discuss this recent incident and the extraordinary dangers that AI poses for humanity.”

The event will feature Geoffrey Hinton, a Nobel Prize-winning computer scientist often called the “godfather of AI;” Max Tegmark, a physicist and co-founder of the Future of Life Institute; and AI researcher Ajeya Cotra, according to the letter, which was later reported by Politico.

The briefing comes as Sanders has escalated his push for Congress to put the brakes on the AI industry.

Last week, Sanders (I-Vermont) and Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas) announced legislation that would permanently prohibit the development and deployment of artificial superintelligence while temporarily pausing the development of advanced AI until a federal regulator establishes safety rules. The bill would also direct the U.S. to pursue international agreements aimed at preventing the development of superintelligence around the world.

The briefing also comes after a viral screed by a former Anthropic researcher who resigned over the company’s “out of control” development. The employee, Jacob Coxon, also worked at OpenAI and said “neither company is acting responsibly.”

“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” Coxon posted on X. “This is not a marketing stunt. If anything, many executives and senior researchers will couch their phrasing in the press to sound sensible — but I hear the same people express fear privately. No other human activity poses this level of danger.”

Sanders has also taken aim at AI companies he views as irresponsibly developing the technology.

In an August letter to the CEOs of Anthropic, Meta and OpenAI, Sanders called on the companies to immediately pause AI development, arguing that they had acknowledged instances in which their systems operated outside their intended safeguards. He warned that companies were racing ahead with technology they could not fully understand or control.

Sanders has also separately pushed for a federal moratorium on new AI data centers, arguing that the rapid construction of facilities needed to power AI is creating costs for communities and workers while the government has yet to establish adequate safeguards.

He and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-New York) introduced legislation in March that would pause construction of new AI data centers until national safeguards are in place. Sanders has argued that the pause would give lawmakers time to address AI’s effects on jobs, electricity demand, the environment, privacy and democracy.

“We cannot allow a handful of billionaires, eager to increase their wealth and power, to rush forward with a technology that will fundamentally transform humanity without democratic input or accountability,” Sanders wrote in an April op-ed.

entries.title: Trump Wants the Census to Stop Collecting Race and Ethnicity Data
entries.summary: The administration wants to stop collecting data widely seen as fundamental to public policy, scientific study, market research and more.
entries.content:
For the first time, the federal government wants to stop collecting race and ethnicity information about Americans as part of the nation’s census, a move that could undercut market research, public policy, scientific study, civil rights enforcement and more.

In a proposal published Wednesday, the Census Bureau argued that collecting demographic data doesn’t advance the “fundamental” purpose of the decennial census to dole out seats in the House of Representatives.

Among its citations for the planned change is the Supreme Court decision that limited states’ ability to draw minority-majority districts by gutting a key section of the Voting Rights Act.

The census proposal confirmed researchers’ fears that President Donald Trump would target race and ethnicity data collection as an extension of the administration's efforts to systematically scrub LGBTQ+ data from government datasets, as The Washington Sun has previously reported.

“The census is our nation’s denominator,” Denice Ross, the U.S. chief data scientist in the Biden administration, told The Sun. It’s the “foundation for all analyses about demographics.”

Prohibiting questions in the decennial census about race, ethnicity or sexual orientation is one half of a sweeping, two-part proposal. The Census Bureau is also proposing to exclude noncitizens without a green card from the population count.

Both changes would have massive implications for the American public.

The removal of many non-U.S. citizens from apportionment data — which would probably be challenged in court — would affect how seats are allocated in the House of Representatives and how Electoral College votes are distributed.

Many states also use federal census data for redistricting, and race and ethnicity data is used to inform public policy, market research and more.

Race and ethnicity breakdowns in maternal mortality data, for example, are difficult to interpret without the baseline provided by the decennial census, said Ross, who now works on federal data policy at the Federation of American Scientists. She worries that other federal agencies will now also stop collecting race and ethnicity data in forms and surveys.

“There’s no substitute for the census data on this,” said Howard Fienberg, the senior vice president for advocacy at the Insights Association, which represents the market research industry.

That industry, he said, relies on demographic data from the census to benchmark studies.

“That’s trillions of dollars in the economy that’s being put at risk if they don’t have the decision-making tools that we’re able to provide,” Fienberg said. “Procter and Gamble is not going to figure out this new breakfast cereal by talking to every single person in the country.”

Scientists also use the race and ethnicity data collected in the census to study things like population aging, adolescent development and more, said MaryJo Mitchell, the director of government affairs for the Population Association of America, which represents researchers like demographers, economists and epidemiologists.

Demographic data from the census is fundamental to even getting started by creating a representative sample, she said.

“We're looking at undoing centuries of standard census practices that have really defined what it means to have a decennial census,” she told The Washington Sun of the proposed changes. Every decennial census, which began in 1790, has included questions on race.

The other half of the new proposal resurrects failed attempts from the first Trump administration to change who is counted in the census.

The Census Bureau proposed adding a citizenship question to the 2020 census, an effort the Supreme Court blocked. Trump also tried in his first term to remove immigrants without lawful status from the apportionment count, although that effort was ultimately not implemented.

The latest proposal would mean that people such as refugees, people seeking asylum, undocumented immigrants and people in the U.S. with work or student visas would not be included in the data used to divide up seats in the House among the states.

How exactly the Census Bureau plans to exclude certain people from its products is unclear.

The Census Bureau says it is considering drawing on records across the government, including information housed at the Department of Homeland Security, as well as commercial data to determine people’s legal status.

Accurately linking up different datasets is extremely difficult, however, said Beth Jarosz, the vice president of the Association of Public Data Users, meaning that U.S. citizens could be flagged as noncitizens if the Census Bureau undertakes this data-matching exercise.

“They would absolutely, in essence, disenfranchise people accidentally,” Jarosz said.

The proposal also says the Census Bureau “could” add a question about legal status on the census questionnaire itself.

Research has found that adding a citizenship question to the decennial census would reduce the number of respondents and disproportionately affect populations that are already hard to count, like those without documentation.
